sumMER GLOOM.

It is the noon of -summer, and the morn Of day, yet mist and clouds o'erhang the scene, And even Nature's glorious garb of green Seems soiled, and raiwbespattered, and forlorn: Such the drear aspect by the landscape worn; • But sun-gleams soon shall flash these clouds between, • Throw over dale and hill a golden sheen, And every object with new charms adorn. So, o'er the heyday of a happy life. Sometimes are cast dark clouds of pain or grief, Dim mists of sorrow, pelting showers of strife; Tintil some heaven-sent gleam brings kind relief, Scattering the gloom that marred life's summer day. Whilst thankful gladness owns the Sun- God's sway. July, 1881. D.

DAISIES IN THE CITY. Away from the soil that bore them, Away from the waving grass, Away from the winds that kissed them Down in the meadow pass, Away from the sun that gave them Their hearts of yellowest gold, Away from the tears of heaven, And the love they nightly told Away from the song of the skylark, Away from the song of the rain, Away from the song of the reaper's scythe As it sweeps through the golden grain, Away from the song of the whirring bee, As it seeks the purple clover, Away from the song of the farmer's lass, As she sings of her farmer lover: Away from the smile of the summer sky, Sweet recollect lUDS bringing, For in the shadow of these walls I hear the throstle singing; And I see the face of Nature glow With haunt lnitier the b scenes otreasures; earlier y Anears, And pursue roy childhood's pleasures. And many eyes are filled with tears— When in my casement spying These messengers from scented fields— And many hearts witlh, havesighing; caught And some, perhaps, as From out their fragrance spreading, The incense which the fairer flowers In heavenly fields are shedding.
Varitties.

The Own*r of a toy watch called it Faith, because it was without works, and therefore dead. Gold can hay pretty nearly everything in this world ex- cept that whit% a man wants most—viz., happiness. He is a very ordinary man who never finds fault with himself, and a very extraordinary one who never has reason tc do so. It is beautiful to gather about the domestic fireside, but the tire our.ht to be on the hearthstone and not in the temners.of those who live there. In a recent article on a fair in the locality, the editor of a Western paper says a brother editor took a valuable pre- mium, but an unkind policeman made him put it right back where he t ,ok it limn. A -well, whose solvency is not so irreproachable as is his linen, has a dozen tailors at least, although the number of his garments is not large. Some one asked him why SO masy. "You see, I don't like," he says, "to have the loss all fall of -me." The mot: of revising the Massachusetts statutes is in pro- ,e;ress. Perhaps it was in anticipation of this work that the Great and General Court once voted to have the old papers in the State-House re-arranged, and to have new copies made of such as were found to he illegible. Cow-catchers are not needed on the electric railway mo- tors in Prussia. A horse which stepped on one of the rails was thrown down, and another suffered a shock that sent it galloping away in terror. Deaf men will be able to indulge their propensity for walking on the track by wearing'Shoea with indiarahher soles. A prisoner who has been convicted at least a dozen times is placed at the bar. "Your honour, I should like to have my case postponed for a week. My lawyer is ill." "But you were captured with your hand in this gentleman's pocket. What can your counsel say in your defence?" " Precisely so, your honour. That is what lam curious to know." In a foreign settlement east of the Cape of Good Hope there lived, not many wears ago, a person whom the rude public called "the self-made man." They always insisted that he put himself together in the morning—inserted his glass eye and his false teeth (some said added an artificial rose), adjusted his wig, strapped on his wooden leg—and sallied forth. It happened that trouble broke out between the country to which he belonged and the one in which he was living; and it was then and there reported that he had gone to the United States Consul and claimed protection. On being asked on what he founded his claim, he promptly replied that his leg was made of Oregon pine. and an Arneri- Con dentist made his teeth. MEW

DErtsirriox OF Sucurat.—Cert iinly a large proportion and the best of the pleasantries in the Drawer come from and are about of the clergy. Here is one of the Rev. Mr. , who had taken into his service, for general utility, a poor lad, and for whose spiritual welfare he was, of course, bound to look out. Desiring one morning to put in practice fin beney .lent intent, he called the boy to his study, and with visage of the gravest sort, said, "Sam, do you know you are a sinner?" "Yes," falteringly replied Sam. "Do you know what will become of you, if, you do not repent?" Receiving no coherent reply, he launched into repentance and redemption, encouraged by the evident impression made by his words, and feeling no small compunction the while that he bad so long neglected a "subject of grace" no promising. At last a vacant and wandering look roused a sudden suspicion, to verify which he inquired, "Sam, wnat is is sinner?" Imagine the situation when the "sub- ject if grace" promptly reiponded, "Sinner, Sir? Yes, air; sinners is strings in turkeys legs, sir." The sinews of toei parson's face relaxed.—Harper's Monthly. Tux BENEFITS or REGULAR Livirsu.—A great deal might be said about tfie benefits of regularity in our modes and ways of living. As a proof of the beneficiality of regular living., I may instance the fact that old people who have once se tled down in a hind of groove of life, if I may. so call it, cannot he unsettled therefrom even for a few days without danger to health and life itself. They may have, perhaps, their regular time for getting up in the morning, 1, certain methods of ablution, certain kinds and qualities of food and drink, certain hours for taking these, certain times for rest, exercise, and recreation, and a hundred other things, which, taken s 0 .arately, may seem but trifles, but taken in the aggregate make up their lives, and they know and feel that they must not be unsettled. The wheels of life will run long in grooves, but soon run out over rough irregular roads. tlabirs, whether good or bad, are easily formed when one is' young, but when one gets up in years it is terrifily difficult and of tames dangerous to set them aside. There- fore, I say to the young—av, and to the middle-aged—study, if you would live long, to be regular in your habits of life n every way, and let your regularity have a good tendency. —Cassell's 'Amity Magazine.

GEORG?, STrATHEN/lON AND THE BIRDL—On one occasion the acznr icy of his (Stephenson's) knowledge of birds came flea in a curious w iv, at a convivial meeting of railway men i• London. The engineers and railway directors present kaew each other as railway men, and nothing more. The td.k had tle-n all of railways and rail way politics. Mr. Stephens in was avgreat talker on these subjects, and was generally allowed, from the interest of his conversation and the extsot of his experience, to take the lead. At length one of the party broke in with, "Come, now, Stephenson, we have bad nothing but railways; cannot we have is c,,Ange, and try if we can talk a little about something •," Well," 8 dd Mr. Stephenson," I'll eive von a wide range of subjects; what shall it be about t"" Say birds' nests," rejoined the other, who prided himself on his special ,kn..wledge of this subject. "Then MlAs' nests be it." A 14 g and animated conversation ensued ; the bird-nesting of nis Isiyhood, the blackbird's nest which his father had- held . Dien up in his arms to look at when a child at Wylani, the uedge in which be found the thrush's and the linnet's nest., the moss bank where the robin built, the cleft in the branch Of the young tree in which the chaffinch had reared its dvielling•—all rose up clear in his mind's eye and led him ba •Ic to the scenes of his boyhood at Callerton and Dewley B.an. The colour anti number of the hircls' eggs, the period of their incubation, the materials ediployed by them for the wills and lining of their nests—were described by him so vividly, and illastrated by such graphic anecdotes, that one of the party remarked that if tieorge Stephenson had not !haul the greatest engineer of his day, he might have been one of the greatest naturalists. Ties COASTGUARD ON Dory.—Let us look at the coast- gnarurnan in winter, and such a winter as our last one—let • us i•ee him turn out at midnight, and invest himself in his heavy night hoots, his thick piiot-cloth coat, yards of com- forter toned his neck, and over all, oilskin leggings, coat, .and a te-wester. Let us watch him as he plods his three or four miles. in the teeth of a bleak nor'-eaeter to make his :meeting at 3 am ,all the time keeping his '6 weather eye" open seawards, to catch the first glimmer of an unusual light, or listening to what sounds like the paying out of a chain ca,,le, as some vessel, finding herself in .shoal water, Sets go her anchor for fear of drifting on shore. Then see how spry and lively he becomes, how he hastens to give the , alarm to. his chief, or probably to render assistance per- , • sonally:, lie uncaps the bead of his port-fire, which he always carries on,night duty, strikes it upon a stone or the roe of his sboe, and immediately a bright blaze Surrounds itn, which will last for twenty enhautea. Ele then fires his revolver to attract the attention of others of his comrades, they slyo the station," and scion All is a ticentl of hurry and hustle. rt:e thief is commnticated with, and he 'turns an. experienced eye to the wind and weather, and calculates the exact height of the tide, and whether it is ebbing or flow- ing. De fortis an oninion as to the roughness of the sea, and after a moment's thought gives the word "apparatus." Then the old mortar, which has lain quietly in a corner perhaps for months, is brirught out, a charge of powder' ihttortuceit, ind a' match .applied. Bang! goes the piece,: etartling the villagers in their cosy beds: They know the Sound, and creep out one by one into the cold night, to fall Into their respective places, ready to render all the assist- ance in their power.—From " Litde Folks Magazine" for Jul.

A story is told of El Mehdi, one of the Abbasides, that, being out hunting one day, he came upon the hut of an Arab, who set some simple fare before him, but supplemented it with a bottle of wine. The Caliph drank a glass, and said, "0 brother of the Arabs! do you know who I am ?" "No, by Allah!" was the reply. "I am one of the personal attendants of the Commander of the Faithful." "I con• gratulate you on your post," said the other. Tossing cd another glass Eli Mehdi repeated the question, and the Arab reminded him that he had just told him he was one of the Caliph's suite. "Nay," said El Mehdi, "but lam one of his principal officers." "I wish you joy !" said the Arab. After a third glass, the Caliph again began, "0 brother of the Arabs! do you know who lam ?" "You say that you are one of the Commander of the Faithfol's chief officers," answered the Arab. "Not so," said El Mehdi, "I am the Commander of the Faithful himself !" The Arab, on hear- ing this, quietly took the bottle of wine from the table, and put it away, with the sententious remark, "If you were to drink another glass, you would declare that you were the prophet himself." NEW VERSION OF THE MIRACLE OF LOAVES AND FtstrEs.—Before the late struggle it was customary for large landholders in Virginia to elect one negro to a more op.rous and important position than the rest—namely, to saperintend the others in the various branches of labour. A certain sable individual promoted to this responsibility was no Bayard in point of honour, and had no qualms of conscience in shirking his duty on any cOnvenient oppor- tunity. His master shrewdly suspected that Jim's frequent requests to attend " meetin' " were not instigated by reli- gious fervour, but that frolics of a more mundane character were the objects of these weekly petitions. With these ana- -1 picions strong in his mind, he gave him leave one afternoon to go to" meetin'." On the following morning he proceeded to question him in relation to what he had heard: "Well, Jim, where was the meetin' held ?" "Why, marster, up at Dry and Hungry.'" "Who preached, Jim "Old Mr. Huyarn. rowed ul preacher, marster—po werful." "What did he preach about ?" "be maracle, marster." "But what miracle, Jim ?" " Dat ar' miracle, marster, 'boat de loaves and de fishes." "What did the preacher say about it?" "Well, you see, old muster, de Saviour had been preachin' and teachin', and de twelve 'postles was wid him: and de 'pestles dey got hungry, and thar wa'n't nothin' that to eat but one or two loaves.and one or two little bits of fishes; so de Saviour he blessed dem and dar was five thousand loaves and five thousand fishes, and de 'postles dey went and eat.'em all up." "But, Jim, I think you've got that wrong." "No, I ain't marster—no I ain't. You don't onderstand ; de maracle was, dat de 'pestles eat up all de loaves and all de fishes, and dey didn't bust !"—Harper'. Monthly.

THE LONDON AND COUNTRY CHURCRES.—The Liberator of this month, after reviewing the scandalous state of the London City churches, with their immense revenues and almost no congregations—the incumbents, with all their great wealth, preaehing to substantially empty benches, Pave:—" But we have an impression that this state of things is not altogether peculiar to the City of London. A commission sent to the rural districts Would probably elicit similar facts, and show that the Church, as regards attend- ance, which .is the indication of membership more or less attached, commands as little support there as it does in the heart of the city. It is a name, and not a reality." A "POOR ORPHAN GIRL."—At Bow-street police court (London), on Monday, as the court was about to rise, Miss Wilberforce, the plaintiff in the late action of "Wilberforce v. Philp," approached the witness box, and addressing the magistrate, said " Sir, I am a poor orphan girl, thousands of miles from home and friends, the victim of a foul conspiracy. My enemies are both rich and power- ful, and even now are seeking to drive me into the ranks of the criminal classes. I implore you to help me. Mabel Wilberforce stands before you." This was said with the most impassioned gestures, while tears fell from the eves of the applicant. Mr. Flowers said he regretted his inability to help her in the matter, on which Miss Wilberforce re- tired. THE Poon CLERGY.—The poverty of the poor clergy would be bard to bear in any case, but what must be the feelings of a poor curate when he hears of such: a living as that of Wimbstsb. Essex, the net income of which is £650 a year. while "no duty whatever" is required from the holder! It has been a sinecure for more than 400 years, and for the most part has been bought by ladies for family purposes. It is also a donative—i.e., the right to present is absolute, and any clergyman, whatever his character, can be presented, "in spite of all the bishops in England." This living was lately Rut up to auction, and, not being sold, the price is reduced horn £6,200 to £5,500. It is an investment simply—we cannot say pure and simply.—Libemtor. The new Reform Club at Oldham was on Monday opened by the Earl of Dalhousie, who was very cordially welcomed by the Liberals of the borough. His lordship at a public meeting in .the evening defended the Government in a very effective speech in the matter of the Parliamentary Oaths Bill and the Transvaal peace., Upon the latter subject, after tracing the course of events `rom the time of the annexa- tion, and showing the Home Government had been deceived with regard to the Boers' disposition to accept British rule, he said that Mr. Gladstone's Ministry resolved upon a change of policy before our troops met with the first of the reverses which they suffered. When, therefore, their op- ponents said that the 'Government made peace in conse- quence of these reverses, they said that which was not in accordance with the facts. To have gone on fighting under the circumstances would have been, to use Mr. Gladstone's emphatic phrase, to involve this country in " sheer blood- guiltiness." LORD CAIRNS ON PROTESTANTISM IN IRELAND.—EarI Cairns presided on Wednesday at a meeting in London to raise funds to assist the poor parishes in the south and west of Ireland. He said that when the church was disestablished means were taken by which the various districts of the country were assisted, and funds were paid from the central body in proportion as the assets were paid in these districts. In the north no difficulty had been experienced, but in the south and west particularly, in consequence of the land agitation, the landlord had been unable to pay the assets ; consequently the clergy had lost half their income, and hail to look for the other half to a breach of rules on the part of the central authority. Unless some help was rendered in Parishes where the Protestant population was small, Protestantism would cease to axis', and disloyalty, dark- ness, and disorder would take the place of it. Resolutions supporting the object of the meeting were passed, and sub- scriptions to a considerable amount announced. Mr. Bradlangh, addressing on Monday a crowded audience at the Hall of Science, London, said he believed that Mr. Gladstone would !Lye carried or tried to carry the Parliamentary Oaths Bill had be deemed it possible. He believed that the Premier only abandoned it because he h Id no choice between the abandonment of that measure and the more than possible risk of losing the whole of the work that had been expended upon the Irish Land Bill. The hon. member had to fight for himself and decide for himself, and he would tell them what he was going to do. He asked them to meet in Trafalgar Square on Tuesday, the 2nd day of August for the purpose of protesting against any altera- tion of the law, and for the purpose of insisting that the law as it stood should be carried out. That would be a perfectly legal gathering. For organising and conducting the meeting he wanted 500 stewards. He proposed going to the table of the House of Commans—if he did not go before—on Wednesday, 3rd August. when the Irish Land Bill would be through the House. He should do nothing illegal. Those who defied the law at present were the 210 members who, by physical force, stood between him and his seat. COLLAPSE OE AN EXTRAORDINARY LIBEL CASE.—An aotion brought by a woman calling herself Mabel Wilber- force collapsed on Monday. Plaintiff formerly resided with Dr. Philp, an old gentleman now deceased, and she insti- toted these proceedings with the view of vindicating what she calls her character from libellous aspersions :alleged to have been cast upon it by Captain Philp, Dr. Philp's RCM. On Thursday Miss Wilberforce desired to withdraw a num- ber of statements she had advanced the day before, modestly pleading that the mistakes must be attributed to her nervolsness. On Friday Miss Wilberforce was ill in bed, and was not in attendance. On Monday she again presented herself in court; but her counsel announced that they must withdraw from the case in consequence of the receipt of a telegram from America, discrediting her con- stant references to a Mr. Oliver Perry Morton, whom she described as her acting trustee, but who, so far as can be , ascertained, died in 1877. His lordship, in directing a ver- dict for the defendant, said be was satisfied that the plaihtiff had produced fabricated documents for the purps,se of carrying out a most infamous design against Captain Philp. The letters and documents put in by the plaintiff were orderect to be impounded. THE BISHOPS AND THE LIBERATION SOCIETY.—They do I not say that Liberationists wish to turn cathedrals into drinking saloons, and churches into chapeis—though Dr. Magee says that some of them do so wish—their contention is, that when Parliament and the parishes have full control over these ecclesiastical edifices, they may possibly be applied to such uses. Of course they may, and of course they might be so applied at this moment if public opinion sanctioned it. It has sanctioned the pulling down of some c'ty and other churches, and warehouses, if not factories, have been erected on the sites. Ths fact, however, is that these bishops, and others who talk, and write in this fashion, have no fear in the matter themselves; though they try to inspire others'with fear. They know the character of the English people, and even the character of Liberators, too well to have any teach fears. But the fears are affected, as a means of frightening those who do not know better. It is not a high-minded way of defending the Establishment, and not worthy of Christian men and bishops; but when men are placed is a false position, and have to depend on an in- defensible institution, they are at to lose a tine sense of what is right, and to do that which seems most likely to blacken and to thwart its opponents.—Liberator.

div.head: HER MAJESTY'S PRIME MINISTERS.
div.p: HER MAJESTY'S PRIME MINISTERS.
THE RIGHT HON. W. E. GLADSTONE.

On resigning the seals of office in 1874, Mr. Gladstone expressed a wish to retire from the leadership of the Liberal Tarty in the House of Commons. Writing to Lord Gran- ville on January 13th be announced his completedetermina- tion to retire after 42 years of a laborious life, adding that this retirement was dictated to him by his personal views as to the" best method of spending the closing years of my life." His opponents, however, were pleased to regard this determination as the natural result of 'a ruffled temper and a disappointed ambition, and riot to a conviction which he had that his work as leader was done, and to a very natural desire for rest. When in 1879 he reached the age of three score years and ten, and the Liverpool Liberal Association presented to him with their congratulations, a handsome silver casket, Mr. Gladstone, in acknowledging their kind- ness said : " I was truly anxious six years ago to withdraw myself from the sphere of party contention. Whether rightly or wrongly, I conceived the idea that more than 40. years of service to my country in a public station, made it rational, becoming, and in every way appropriate for me to ask for my dismissal." During tbe first three Sessions of the last Parliament, Mr. Gladstone remained in the shade— his voice being rarely heard in that Hall which had so fre- quently rung with its eloquence. But there are times in a nation's history, crises, when a high sense of duty, when a strong conviction of what is right and just, when a clear view of personal responsibilities will compel a man to trample underfoot all considerations of ease and pleasure. Silence then is no longer golden. He " cannot but speak" the thrilling truths which reign and glow in the centre of his heart. You may as well attempt to arrest the whirl- wind, or roll back the planets, as to silence the man whose heart throbs responsive to the call of duty. It was so with Mr. Gladstone. An honest man himself—one whom
Neither gold Nor sordid fame nor hope of heavenly bliss

could attempt to deviate a hair's breadth from what he con- ceived to be the right, as soon as he saw the Government departing from the Policy of Burleigh and Raleigh, of Blake and Cromwell, of William of Orange and Chatham, of Canning and Palmerston, the policy of rectitude and liberty, and adopting a policy of cynic selfishness' which ignored honour and trampled upon right, then Gladstone with "dauntless words and high" did speak, as did he Who shook the sere leaves from the woods As if a storm swept by. "It was the peculiar nature of the Eastern Question" says he "which first made me feel it an imperative duty to modify the resolution at which I had arrived, not so far as regarded my position in the Liberal party, but so far as re- garded the amount of my personal activity." The history of Tory misrule which Mr. Gladstone from time to time so eloquently denounced need not detain us here. The nation was under the sway of those who "were the men and the political heirs of the m n who passed the Six Acts and the Corn Laws, who impoverished the popu- lation, who fettered enterprise by legislative restraints, who withheld those franchises that have given voice and vent to the public wishes, whose policy in a word kept the Throne Insecure, anti the Empire weak, and would, unless happily arrested in 1832 and again in 1848, have plunged the country in Revolution ;' and the sources from whence the Ministers drew their strength were "not peace, not humanity, not reverence for the traditions' eltablished by the thought and care of. the mighty dead, not anxiety to secure the equal rights of nations, not the golden rule to do to others as we would fain have them do to us, not far seeing provision for the future." (Nineteenth Century, Sept., 1878.) At length the Ninth Parliament of her Majesty's reign, and the "worst of modern Parliaments," was dissolved after in inglorious existence of something more than six wears. Prior to the Dissolution Lord Beaconsfield issued a mani- festo—notninally addressed to the Lord-Lieutenant of Ire- land, but in reality intended for the constituencies—a letter which consisted of "mystery and nonsense," according to the Saturday Belden', which was characterised by the Lon- don Echo as "a masterpiece of misrepresentation and audacity," and which WAS only possible from the pen of the man who all his public life had acted with undeviating constancy upon the maxim which he put into the mouth of one of his own ficticious characters—" With words we rule men." Having stated that the measures affecting Ireland were about to be submitted for the Royal Assent, and that . . . . .

the way was therefore cleared for a dissolution, the Premier denounced the Home Rule movement, and mysteriously re- ferred to "some" who "challenge the expediency of the Imperial character of this realm," who have sought to en- 1 feeble the Colonies by "their policy of decomposition," and 1 who perhaps think they can accomplish their purpose by "the disintegration of the United Kingdom." In the last paragraph, Lord Beaconafleld declared that "peace rests on the presence, not to say the ascendancy of England in the . Councils of Europe," and wound up by expressing the hope that whatever might become of her Majesty's advisers a Parliament would be returned "not unworthy of the power I of England, and resolved to maintain it." Varied, however, as were the opinions respecting this "Marlborough Letter." there was one sentence in it which was endorsed by all. "Rarely," said his lordship of Elughenden, "Rarely in this century has there been an occasion more critical. The power of England and the peace of Europe will largely depend upon the verdict of the , country." That statement the country endorsed. The occa- sion was critical. England was in one of the crises of her history. She had fallen upon evil times. A check had been put to her progress. The beneficent flow of her develop- ment had been interrupted, and a new point of departure had been inserted. Her reputation had been sullied, and she had been turned aside from her destiny. And the ques- tion which the English people were called upon to decide was, "Shall this new stafh of things continue and govern England's future It Shall we accept another term of Beaconsfieldian rule, with its bloodstained policy abroad, leading to depression and distress at home, or shall there be a return to the old Gladstonian lines along which the Nation once moved when her path seemed to toe like that of the sun, "shining more and more unto the perfect day," and over which there floated the banner with this device, "Peace, Retrenchment, Reform, Religious Equality." That was the issue before the country. Never within the memory of man perhaps had there been a General Election at which the at- tention of the people had been AO fully concentrated on one point. Again and again did The Times complain that the Liberals had no programme, and that their only cry was, "Turn out the Government." That wig the cry which the country adopted with acclamation. Stronghold after strong- hold of Conservatism fell before the gallant attacks of Liberalism. Positions which had hitherto been deemed in- vulnerable by their Tory defenders passed into the hands of the Party of Progress, and it soon became evident that the Beaconsfield Administration must either perish by voluntary resignation, as in 1868 before the meeting of Parliament. or be driven from office by a vote of censure immediately after the House of Commons had been organised. Lord Beacons- field resolved upon the former, and without any unnecessary . loss of time resigned into the hands of his Royal Mistress hi a seals.of office. No sooner had Lord Beaconsfield tendered his resignation than it became an absorbing question "Who would the Queen send for ?" The choice of the Crown was practically between three names—those of Lord Granville, Lord Hart- ington, and Mr. Gladstone; but the prior place unquestion- ably must be assigned to the last. To him was due the immense impulse by which the Liberal forces were ani- mated, and the active energy of the party was to a large extent concentrated in him. This" sophistical rhetorician, Inebriated with the exuberance of his own verbosity," had pricked the bubble of Imperialism and had overthrown his great rival. It was clear therefore that no Liberal Cabinet could be formed without Mr. Gladstone at its head. When Achilles showed himself on the wall the whole host felt that he was the Greek champion, and that the kings of the House of Atreus could not hold candle to him. In like man- ner the great mass of Liberals felt that whatever were the claims of Lord Granville and the Marquis of Hartington, Mr. G-ladstone's were paramount. Not so apparently thought her Majesty. Hence Lord Hartington was first sent for, but he failing to impress her Majesty with the con- viction that he was both unable and unwilling under the circumstances to construct a Cabinet, repaired next morn- ing to Windsor, accompanied by Earl Granville. They both had an audience of the Queen, and must have submit- ted to her Majesty their conviction that Mr. Gladstone alone could successfully preside over a new Liberal Ministry. The Queen, on being thus informed of the real circum- stances of the political situation, acted promptly with that faithful regard for constitutional duty which she .has in- variably displayed, and Rent at once for the statesman who was the real leader of the victorious party at the elections, and without hesitation or reserve entrusted him with the duty of conducting her Government. Ever attentive to the voice of the Nation and the wish of his Sovereign, Mr. Gladstone accepted the duty, designating himself for the office of Chancellor of the Exchequer in addition to that of First Lord of the Treasury, and he kissed hands on receiv- ing both appointments. The Cabinet was soon constituted., • and the announcement that a Liberal Administration had taken possession of Downing-street was hailed with accla- mation throughout the length and breadth of the land. It • was felt that England would be law-abiding, Christian Eng- land once more, and not the Alsatia of Europe—the play- ground of the swashbuckler and adventurer. It was felt that thb ship of State, after a pitiless tossing on the storm-lashed ocean, was now commanded by a pilot who would float it into peaceful waters, and a sense of relief took possession of the hearts of men The Liberal Government commenced its duties, however, , heavily handicapped. it succeeded to a legacy of debt at o home and difficulty abroad, but already it has succeeded to some extent in paying the one and meeting the other. This 5 thoroughly accomplished. grand, and beneficent legislative achievements will follow for William Ewart Gladstone—the Christian statesman who has demonstrated that simplicity t of character and moral sensibility are not incompatible with , true political greatness—" forgetting the things that are be- hind, and reaching forth unto those that are before," will saY to those whom he has so often led to victory the stir- ) ring words which Tennyson has put into the month of Ithaca—

Souls that have toiled and wrought and thought with me; That ever with a frolic welcome took The thunder and the sunshine and °lmo*. Free hearts, free foreheads, you andl are old. : Old age hath yet its honour and its toil; • Death closes 1111, but something ere the end— Some work of noble note may yet be done Not unbecoming men that strove with gods. , Come, my friends, 'Vs not too late to seek a newer world.

We now bring our sketches of her Majesty's Prime Minis- ters to a close. Only the other day her Majesty completed the 44th year of her beneficent reign, and during that period, while she has had only nine Parliaments, she has presided over the formation of no fewer than fourteen Administrations. It seems a long time hack when the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Lord High Chancellor I called in early morning at Kensington Palace, in order to announce the death of William IV. to the young Princess Victoria, and to pay homage to her as Sovereign Ruler of a I powerful empire. We have not space to mention, much less dilate upon, the many changes in connection with the social , advancement, commercial prosperity, art, science, and literature, education, and material progress of the Nation which have taken place since then. The last half century, more than any of its predecessors, has been fruitful of scientific discovery, mechanical progress, spread of learning, philanthropic enterprises, and religious development. The "golden age," for the coming of which good men have toiled and suffered and died, may yet be a great way off. But surely it is coming. "The former times were not better than these." As Festus save, " 'Tis better than it once was, and bath more of mind and freedom than it ever had." The many no longer suffer for the few. The toil-worn labourer" renews his strength by food at once abundant and untaxed," and relishes it all the better "because no longer embittered by any feeling of injustice." The degradation has been removed from the brow of the Dissenter, the Catholic, and the Jew, which priestcraft had planted there. The facilities for communication and intercourse with dis- tant people have been multiplied and cheapened by means of ' the Post, the Telegraph, and the Railway. Slaves have lacorne citizens. Serfs are growing into men. Institutions with every charitab,e purpose are now supported by volun- tary Contributions. The health of the community is the care of the community as it has never been before. Educa- tion is the common birthright of all. "Freedom broadens slowly down from precedent to precedent." The Sovereign is no longer surrounded by "pimps, panderers, and volup- tuaries." No longer in speaking of the Court need we adopt the language of the Prince of Denmark and say "Virtue itself of Vice must pardon beg." Throughout a long reign her Majesty has worn "the white feather of a blameless life," and the First Lady of the Land is as much beloved and honoured as ever she was. From stately Cathedral and Nonconformist Sanctuary—from the gorgeous Church and the plain Meeting House on every Sabbath day the cry goes up to Heaven in perfect sincerity, " God save the Queen," and we cannot conclude these sketches better than by expressing the fervent wish that her Majesty's future Prime Ministers and Statesmen may over be like those described by our Poet Laureate—

And Statesmen at her Council met Who knew the seasons, when to take Occasion by the hand, and make The bounds of freedom wider yet, By shaping some august decree, Which kept her throne unshaken still, Broad based upon her people's will, And compass'd by the inviolate sea.

THE VOLUNTEER, REVIEW AT WINDSOR. The Review by Her Majesty the Queen of Volunteers !It Windsor, OD Saturday, in celt•bration of the 21st year of tne sbe t existence of the Volunteer Force, was a great success. 55.000 volunteers were on the ground, and, with the Oct tion of a few slight showers, the weather was favourable, •I'" was to be expected, the bulk of the troops came from dlesex, Kent, and Surrey. The metropolis and ite • 0. diate neighbourhood sent forth no less than 20,00 50 The 20th Lancashire, from Manchester, numbered, men, having exceeded its estimate by 150, wasthe regiment on the ground. The contingent from La eliat it the Ist, sth, 6th, 20th, and 21st (St. Helens) formed described as the crack brigade of the day. The'Queeei Royal Family arrived on the review ground aboa o'clock, and were received with a Royal salute. The of honour in the march past, which occupied an boar forty minutes, was given to the Royal Naval Volnntv were twelve companies strong, and marched with a e, and precision that were not exceeded during the day• the march past the Royal patty left the . the various regiments proceeded to the dezvous for refreshments, and so successful w,r the way arrangements that by half-past ten o'clock all th teen had left by train, and by eleven Windsor had r its normal appearance. With the exception of 3 shower of rain which fell during the march. Pse" weather was in every respect truly Queen's weather. Duke of Cambridge was in command of the entire it doubtful whether any general has ever commslib. e home or abroad nearly so large a number of men of slt birth as were that day assembled in Windsor fark..("'" previous review has thetas been more than 30.000 ede' under arms, so that Saturday's demonstration Dlr.:, cends in importance and greatness any which he'" ceded it. •er tO The Queen Ims desired the Commander-in-Chi press her entire satisfaction with the soldier-like a' and bearing of all ranks at the review in Windsor notifying this in "general orders," the Due of expresses himself as s ttisfied that the discipline .durance of all ranks would do credit to troops ere permanent service, and are worthy of the highest dation. His Royal Highness also thanks the ;',.ral panics for their hearty to-operation and untiring 'rho Daily Telegraph says :—" 'The fame of ti shire Lads' had preceded them, and we were peri• pared for something extra Ordinary when the Vitt.; under General Spurgin, came up, hut certainly r really wonderful regiment, the 6th Lancashire led the Army Corps. More than a thousand:4, 12 companies, this splendid regiment went by rri`4l and a smartness which could not have been exee'.. say that the people cheered is bat too faintly ae:, enthusiasm with which they were met. They sre'; as a battalion of Guards, and quite astonished 017 and experienced soldier. Percy Lefroy Mapleton was conveyed h Lewes on Saturday morning. Crowds streets and at the railway stations through WI aad "a roar of execrations" saluted WO Heath. div.head: IMP RIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMP RIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

The LATS LORD lIATRERLEY.L--The LORD CKINCELLOR, rsferring to the recent death of Lord Hatherley, who retired from the chancellorship in 1872, said that since their Lord- ships last met one of the greatest ornaments to the House had been lost. He (Lord Selborne) had for 40 years been on terms of personal intimacy with the eminent man who now, in honoured old age, had been taken from them. Per- sonal affection for the deceased would, perhaps, prevent his expressing the sense of loss which was felt by their Lord- ships, but he could say that whilst he (Lord Hatherley) was, ever diligent in the practice of his profession, to the last he retained as much purity and stmplicity of character as any public man could hope to retain. (Cheers.)—Earl Cairns; Earl Granville, and others addressed the House. LONDON BRNEFICES.—The Earl of ONSLOW drew atten- tion to a statement recently published, purporting to be a census of tlie city of London churches, by which it ap- peared that 57 churches within one square mile, having a capacity to seat 31,000 people, only on Sunday the Ist of May had an ordinary congregation of 3,853 persons. The total value of the benaces was over £40,000. His Lordship , moved that a Commission should be appointed to inquirel into the subject with a view of a further union of benefices. —Earl GRiNVILLE thought the subject might be left to the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, and the matter ultimately dropped. •

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDLY. CORPORAL PRNMIINENT IN THE NAVY.-Mr. TREVE‘LYAN announced that the Naval Discipline Act Amendment Bill would not be proceeded with this year, but a circular letter would be issued to commanders-in-chief and senior officers in the navy stating that all the regulations authorising the use of the lash as a summary punishment were to be con- sidered as cancelled.

4.171eC1E UPON MR. FORSTER BY IRISH MEMBERS.—Mr. DALy sited the Chief Secretary for Ireland whether the ' arrest of Mr. John O'Connor, at Cork, on the 4th inst., was ;not due to Mr. O'Connor having advised memlsers of the Irisliconstabulary to resign their positions in that force,: and to emigrate, rather than to assist in evicting from their! homes their fellow countrymen with their families.—Mr.; Fousrust said he could give no answer, except That Mr." O'Connor had been arrested on suspicion of being guilty of treasonable practices—Mr. Loam. moved the adjournment of the House, and Mr. PARNELL seconded the motion.—Mr. T. P.O'Cowxou asked the Prime Minister to convey a mes- sage of peace not only to Ireland, but to Lancashire, by sending his unfortunate colleague" about his business.— Mr. HEALEY described Mr. Forster as "a horrible failure," and Mr. BIGGAR suggested that the rigtt hon, gentleman should be made Secretary for India, as it was desirable that he should be sent to a warmer climate.—Mr. R/CIIARDSON and Mr. MAGARTNEY repudiated this attack on Mr. Forster ; and Mr. GLADSTONE defended his colleague with characteris- tic chivalry, declaring that Mr. Forster was no more respon- sible than were the other members of the Cabinet for coer- cive legislation, whilst no member could claim a greater share of the credit attaching to the ameliorative legislation introduced by the Government.—Sir S. Norrruinorn strongly deprecated the attack, and en a division the motion for adjournment was rejected by 205 votes to 26. MR. FARNELLtS 'IRISH ESTATES.—Mr. LONG offered a personal explanation to the effect that the charges be recently made against Mr. Parnell in respect to the treat- ment of his tenantry really applied to the member for Cork's brother. Mr. Long admitted.that this was "an important' error," and Mr. Parnell strongly protested against the' course pursued by that gentleman in attacking his younger brother under the pretext of a personal explanation. TRE LAND TILL.—The House afterwards went into Com- mittee on the Irish Land Bill, when the considtration of Clause 21, relating to the reclamation of waste lands, was resumed.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS..-TUESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS..-TUESDAY.

COURT OF JUDICATURE BILL.—On the order for reading the Supreme Court of Judicature Bill a second time, Lord' ClemNe, after indicating the parts of the measure which bad his approval, observed that the portion of it which related to the future constitution of the Appellate Court required. serious consideration; for that curt having become the , keystone of our Judicature, it was desirable to strengthen it- and give it solidity and firmness.—The Lora) Cwatqcormott expressed his willingness to postpone that part of the Bill: which related to the selection of three Paine Judges to act as Judges of the Court of Appeal. The Bill was then read a second time.

div.p: HOUSE OF_COMMONS.—TuEsDAy.

THE RUSSIANS IN CENTRAL Asc*. Sir C. DILKE, answering a question from Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, said the Government bad not heard of the occupation by the Russians of Kuchan, in Persian Khorassan; and in answer to Mr. Lahouchere, he said the Foreign Office had no official knowledge of the alleged illegalities at the Bulgarian elections.

MR. FORSTER AND HIS OFFICE.—Mr. Fonsran sail that Parliament had imposed upon bitn a heavy responsibility, and he was quite prepared, if a motion was raised, to meet any charges as to the manner in which he had administered it.—Mr. COWEN (who was reminded by the Speaker that the question had been answered and that he could not argue it' asked if the Government would 'give facilities for such a motion.—Mr. FORSTER said that the hon. member was acquainted with the practice of the House. As to any further facilities, he mast apply to the Prime Minister.

THE ENGLISH SUNDAY CLING STuzarsow, who has charge of the English Sunday Closing Bin, stated that be saw no chance of legislation on the snbject in the present session, and he therefore moved that the order for the second reading of the Bill be discharged, which was ' agreed to. THE IRISH LAND BILL.—The House afterwards resumed Committee on the Land Bill. The amendment by Mr. Lyons, empowering the Land Commission to acquire waste lands and sell them in suitable lots, and the Board of Trade to advance purchase money to the boyers, was vigorously ridiculed by Mr. Gladstone. The Prime Minister said the amendment had not received the support of a single one of the 550 representatives of Scotland and England. As to the argument that the British Government had spent seventeen millions in Afghan wars and might now spend a little Is reclaim the waste lands in Ireland, Mr. Gladstone asited whether the Irish members had endeavoured to prevent these great military outlays. The Irish members were accustomed, the Prime Minister said, to speak AS if they were petitioners at the bar, and had no votes to give along with representatives of the other portions of the kingdom in governing the deliberations of Vata House. The reclamation of waste lands, Mr. Gladstone added, was a perilous enter- prize, which could only be successfully attempted by pri- vate individuals. Yet it was now proposed to carry oo this work wholesale by the worst of all agencies—namely, the I State; and by the State in the worst of al: possible methods —namely, that of finding all the money and commit- ting the execution of the plans to imperfect instruntmts. I —After some further discussion, in the course of which Mr. I NORTNCOTE rather naively remarked, amidst Home Rule cheers, that he would have preferred to disease the matter ' in Dublin without troubling the House at all, Mr. PARNELL i I spoke of the ease of the poor cattier tenants in the west of I Ireland, and hoped the Prime Minister would take it ,into consideration —The PRIME MINISTER promised that if Mr. Parnell would place an amendment upon the paper, hewould consider it in cemmittee.—Mr. LYON'S amendment was ulti- mately rejected without a division, and the clause adopted.' —Clause 20, dealing wilt the question of emigration, WAS next diseussed.—Mr. RATHBONE referred to the success of Father Nugent's scheme for removing starving people from Donegal to America, and appealed to the Irish members not to oppose the system of emigration.—Mr. GrAnsroto ex- pressed the fullest sympathy in the desire of the Irish mem- bers to see their own people happy at borne, and denied that the emigration scheme represented the primary portion of the bill. At the same time, he hoped that the clause, with some modification, would receive the speedy assent of the Commons.—The debate was suspended at the usual time, and was renewed at the evening sitting. 'HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. THE Inon LAND Bir.e.—Committee was resumed on the Irish Land Law (Ireland') Bill. It happened that no Minister had arrived, and Mr. BIGGAR moved to report progress. i —During the discussion of this point the Psime Minister, Mr. Forster, and Mr. Law entered the House, and after a I, short explanation from Mr. Gladstone the motion to report progress was withdrawn.—The emigration clause was then considered, and Mr. GLADSTONE, in the course of the dis- cussion, undertook to place a limit on the sum to be spent In emigration, or to insert words showing that regard mast be had to the desire and consent of the people themselves as to emigration.—Lord It.
