THE CHURCH PATRONAGE BILL —Replying to Mr. Stan- hope, the PREMIER said that, considering, the 'modifications which had been made in the_lphurch Patronage Bill, an op- portunity might possibly belound for the hon. member to prosecute the measure in the plesent session. MR. BIGGAR .AND THE PROMOTERS OF PUBLIC COM- PANIES.—Mr. H. S. NORTHCOTE called upon Mr. Biggar either to withdraw or substantiate the observations which the member for Cavan was reported to have made with regard to the nature of his (Mr. Northente's) connection with a company promoted in Loudon for land speculation,‘ in Canada.—Mr. BIGGAR denied that he had made any per- Ronal attack upon the member for Exeter, but at the sam,- time maid it was notorious that the bulk of the promoters m public companies in the metropolis were simply adven- turers, and he considered that Mr. Northcote was the dupe of designing parties, who used his name and his character fo, the purpose of promoting their dishonest ends.—Mr. GLAD- STONE condemned Mr. Biggar's conduct in the matter, and

div.head: TIIE EXAMINER, SATURbAY, JULY 16, 1881. ALLE6EI), NITTRDER ST. HELENS.
div.p: TIIE EXAMINER, SATURbAY, JULY 16, 1881. ALLE6EI), NITTRDER ST. HELENS.

On Monday night a shocking murder was committed in Pocket Nook, St. Helens. Shortly after ten o'clock a labourer named Edward Foy, residing in Barber-street, went home from work, and finding his wife was not in the kitchen, he went up stairs and found her in bed with the child in her arms. From what the ,poor woman told her mother, who lives in the same house, it appears that Foy struck the woman a severe blow on the head. She got out of bed and hastened down stairs, followed by her husband, who violently cursed her, and again chased her up stairs into her mother's bedroom. She complained to her mother of the violence he had used to her and put bookend to her head as if in great pain. Ha
then raised his hand•and said he would take' her life, at the

same time striking her a blow on the head with his clenched flat, which proved to be fatal, as she died imme- diately afterwards. When the gravity of the situation flashed upon him he went down stairs and hurried out of the house and escaped. Edward Foy is 35 years of age, 5 feet 5 inches in height, of dark complexion with black curly Lair, and slight motistache, and whiskers, chin shaved, roand NH face and pug nose. He is strongly built. He wore a blue frock coat, with velvet collar, and inside pockets dirty tweed trousers, a brown cap, with ears apd low peak, with some tar on the top; an old grey woollen shirt with narrow white stripes; black and grey scarf, and new clasped clogs. The news of the murder soon spread, and a false rumour was cir- culatei that the murderer had been captured and taken into custody. Crowds assembled in the vicinity of Foy's house, and throughout the day tile women discussed the details of the case in the open street.

ARREST AND EXAMINATION OF THE PRISONER. Edward Foy was captured iri Widnes between 10 and 11 o'clock, on Tuesday night, after an exciting chase by P.C. Laing, of • that place. After considerable dodging on the part of the prisoner, he was caught at Widnes Marsh. Pri- soner was brought up before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) on Wednesday morning, and charged with the murder of his wife, firidget Foy. He appeared very cool and collected and betrayed no signs of feeling.—Supt. Johnston said: This man is merely brought up for a remand charged with having, the night before last, at Pocket-Nook, Parr, caused the death of his wife by striking her on the head; and that in the I presence of his mother-in-law, who is now in the box. After I have proved that he did it, I will ask for a remand until the coroner's inquest, which will be opened this afternoon._ Margaret Murphy' an elderly Irishwoman, who gave her evidence in a very dramatic style, said she lived in Barber- street.—SuperintendentJohnston : Do you know the prisoner ? I do.—Who is he? Edward Foy.—Was he the husband of your daughter who is now deceased? Yes.—They lived in the same house with you at 19 Barber-street? Yes.—What did he do when he came home the night before last? Well, have no clock going in the house but I think it was some- time after eleven.—Whert he came home what did he do? Fle came up the stairs; we were in bed. She was in bed, and the baby in the next room to me.—What did you see? Tell us only what you saw and heard. I heard something of a scnfae,•but I did not see it. She went down stairs and he followed her, but whatever he did to herdownstairs I did not see, a: I was in bed. She came upstaigs, and she said, "Oh, the abuse he gave my poor bead belov4." lie followed her ipto roy bedroom, and said "Go out," and I don't know what curses besides. She bias going to go out—(this to the policeman beside her).—Mr. Johnston: Speak to the magis- trate, and not to the policeman.—Witness: I beg your par- ; I don't know who is the magistrate. He doubled his hand and struck her a blow on the head, and she fell down. I leapt out of bed, but I don't know what I said. I did not think he was going to do this, but be gave her one box, and then she was dead. He knocked her down, and she never I opened her eyes nor spoke a ',Ord, but one groan, and she 1 died. 1 was there when she died. Ile went downstairs, and I was afraid very much; and I said to him, "(so away, go 1 away, we will not have another corpse here." And he did go away.—Mr. Brewis; This is quite sufficient for a remand. • (To prisoner.) Have you anything to say why you should I not be remanded? After being asked again, prisoner said, I "I don't know, sir."—Remanded until Friday.

but sod a boy for a 'bottle of medicine. On the following day he went to his work, at the place where I work' antl reached home at five o'clock, but he did not reach home until six o'clock, when he hitt some beer, which .his „irs tent for. lie washed himself and went out, saying he was going to assist his sister-in-law to remove. He came home about eleven o'clock. We had all retired to rest when he came home, and I heard him go into the room, where his wife was, and tell her to get his supper ready. I did not hear her say anything in reply. Immediately afterwards I heard him sty, "By Jesus Christ, I will pull you out of bed." I heard a noise, as if he had pulled her out of bed. I heard her go downstairs, and he followed her at a rapid rate. I thought he would break the stairs on his way down. I could hear him cursing hk Slnd there was a noise as if he was knocking her against the table or a box. She screamed. They were below about ten minutes, and then she cime up- stairs, lie immediately followed her, and came into the room like a madman. She was sitting on the side of our bed, and he said, "Get up out of that. By the Holy Jesus Christ, I will, knock your head off." She stood off, as if to go into her own room. He then struck her a severs blow on the head with his clenched fist. She called out, and her mother stepped between them. Prisoner again gave her a severe Wow on the head, knocked her to the floor, and her head came against the wall as she fell. She did not speak after- wards. She gave one moan and died. I went and lifted her up a little. He was standing at the door, at the time, and said, "By the Holy Jesus Cnrist, if she doesn't get up I will kick her ribs off." I told him that he had finished her, and that she would never get up again. He looked at her for about a minute, and then went downstairs and I didn't see him again till he was in the custody of the police. She did take &ink occasionally, but did not get drunk. He has been addicted to drink ever since I knew him, and has often been out of work, and I had to keep him as well as his wife and family. The Coroner said that was the whole of the evidence they had—it was all that was required for the purposes of an adjournment,and it was for the jurz to decide the day and time to which they would adjourn. The adjourned inquiry was fixed to be held at the Town Hail, on Friday morning, at 11 o'clock.

Foy is spoken of as a very violent aud inconsiderate fel- low, and bears anything but a good character amongst people with whom he has had to-deal both in St. Helens and Widnes, in which latter place he resided previous to his marriage and migration to St. Helens. Between the Town Hall and Pocket Nook is a large waste piece of land in the form of a hillock, and it is said that on leaving the house after the murder he passed over this waste land and waved his hat towards Pocket Nook as a final salute to the place and its inhabitants.. This must, however, be received with

the proverb al grain of salt as the time would be about midnight, and but few people would be stirring. Foy then made in the direction of Widnes, where be camped in lodging houses, The police in that place had been furnished with a description of the man a a copy of which we publish above, and the various members were furnished with slips for their guidance. At St. Helens also the police were exceedingly vigilant. Throughout Tuesday the railway station was closely watched, and every person entering or leaviog the station was closelyscrutinised both by the railway officials and the police, two or three policemen alternately taking the duties of this post. On Tu.sday night P. C. Laiag, of Widnes, found a person who answered to the description given, but before the man could be arrested, a spirited race was necessary, as Foy, seeing hat he was being dogged by the policeman took to his heels tn the direction of Widnes Marsh. P. C. Laing followed, and succeeded in capturing the prisoner, but not Without some dodging on the part q the latter. Foy appeared very cool, and did not deny that he was the man who was wanted. He was brought to St. Helens by a late train and delivered up to the police. He was evidently very hungry as he soon asked for something to eat, which was given him. From further inquiries we glean that Foy had previously threatened fa murder bis wife on several occasions. A woman has exhibited her thumb bearing a knife cut, which she avers was inflicted whilst endeavouring to separate the prisoner and the deceased who were quarrel- ling, the former having a knife in his hand with which be threatened to cut the throat of his wife. He has also been heard to say that he would "swing" for her before long. Much feeling is manifested against the prisoner who seems to be one having but few friends. The deceased has always borne the character of a respectable woman, and of late she has suffered greatly from extreme weakness, and been attended by Dr. Doonellan. The nature of the verdict to be given by the coroner's jury will depend in a great measura on the evidence of the doctor. The prisoner will be brought before the magistrates on Friday morning and formally remanded until Saturday. After the remand on Friday he will be taken before the coroner and jury. .-. . .

. . . At the Red Lion Hotel, before the arrival of the coroner, I the father and mother of deceased, both old and little people, wandered from room t cepm in the hotel, despite the efforts of the police to keep aim still. At times the old man would come to the door and gaze mournfully upon the crowd i assembled outside, and then would return inside' mattering to himself. The crowd expressed great sympathy with the old paople. Finding that it was impossible to keep the old woman still before she was called into the room before the I jury to give evidence, the superintendent of police gave her i a seat and commanded her to keep still whilst the jury were i' viewing the body in another room. She looked very de- , jected, and when asked if she had anything to add to her ; evidence replied that she had neither anything,,to add nor , anything to take from her depositions. The ogi man was I very talkative and rapidly informed the coroner and the pry ( that his had been "a poor life," and from, his appearance he certainly looked like one who stood the brunt of the battle. The crowd outside the hotel expected that the prisoner would be present at the inquest, but in this they were dis- appointed. The prisoner, since his confinement in the cell has mani- feste I the utmost coolness and unconcern. He is being watched night and day by the police. There is great excite- ment in the district where prisoner resided, and the subject of the murder is the constant topic of conversation.

div.head: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.
Fl2lDAY.—Before the Mayor and Mr. H. S. Hall.

ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLE.—WiIIiam Leather, a power- ful young fellow, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly. and with assaulting P.C. Kendal, on Monday night. Prisoner had been at a house in Vincent-street for some money that be alleged was due to him, but the money was refused, and a disturbance ensued. The officer then came upon the scene and took prisoner into custody; the prisoner struck the officer and tore his coat.—Prisoner, who had been several times convicted, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk, and 10s. and costs for the assault upon the constable. A DISGRACEFUL Row.—John Langley, William Langley, and James Langley were charged with committing a breach of the peace in Windle, on Saturday evening. William and James Langley, who had respectively 16 and 17 Convic- tions recorded against them, were bound over themselves in £lO and two sureties of £5 each; and John Langley was bound over in his own recognisances to keep the peace for three morths.—Tames Langley was charged with assaulting Martha Thompson at the same time.—Complainant said her husband and defendant were fighting, and when she inter- fered and beseeched him not to "punch" her husband, he replied that he would do the same to her; and knocked her down and "punched" her—Defendant denied the charge, and said the complainant attacked him with a brick.—The Bench slid one appeared to be as bad as the other, and dis- missed the case.

STEALING A WORKMAN'S WAGES. John Cunliffe (14) son of a publican, residing at Haydock, was again charged with stealing 14s. 84., the property of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers. As stated in our last issue, the prisoner, who worked at Messrs. Pilkington's polishing rooms, received John Topping's tally from the clerk, and on presenting it to the pay-clerk received Topping's money.—Prisonet's mother appeared, and said he had "played truant.," but apart from this she had no fault to find with him.—He was fined £3, which was paid. A DISGRACEFUL SUNDAY PROCEEDING —Charles Scott and John Arnold, youths residing at Parr, were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting on Sun- day last. —Superintendent Johnston said this was a rather serious case; infect it was a prize tight, and lasted for about an hour, defendants bAng stripped to the skin with the ex- ception of trousers. The fight was witnessed by about 100 people, and though attempts were made to stop them the efforts put forth in this direction were tnsuccessfni.—John Kerfoot, horse keeper, residing in Fleet-lane, Parr, said de- fendants were fighting near some waggon works when he came t.pon the scene at ten minutes to one, and he left them at ten minutes past. About 100 people were around them, and they were as had as the fighters.--Thomas Pen- nington, underlooker at Fleet-lane Colliery, said he watched defendants for seven or eight minutes. He tried to separate them, but failed.—Defendants pleaded guilty, but each of them referred to a quarrel that had taken place between them on the previous night, and which went to show that the fight was pre-arranged.—Arnold bore the appearance of having come off second best.—Defendants were each ordered to be bound over in £lO and two sureties of .f. 5 each, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. A DEAR VIEW OF A Recs.—Barney 'Quinn, Parr, was charged with damaging a wall, the property of Henry Burrows. The wall in question is made of chemical waste, and surrounds a race ground, to which a charge for admis- sion is made. On Saturday, whilst a race was being rnn, 'defendant mounted the wall in a recently-repaired part, to i watch the race, and whilst standing upon it the wall fell, I doing damage to the extent of a shilling.—William Wotezey, employed to watch the wall, having given evidence, defen- ' dant was fined 9s. altogether.

Sap:Wm.—Before the Ex-Mayor (Alderman Harrison). DISTURBING THEIR. PEACEFUL SLUMBERS: LEN/ENT SENTE:sCH.—Bprnard Lamb, a young fellow residing at Ste- ton. was charged with being on the premises of John Taylor,! Baxter's-lane, Sutton, on the previous night 'or a felonious purpose.—Sarah Clark, an elderly woman, residing with her son-in-law, said that at a quarter-past eleven she fastened the doors and went to bed. About two o'clock she heard a noise downstairs as if someone were pulling clogs off, and directly afterwards she hoard someone coming up stairs, and she saw the prisoner enter the bedroom without jacket or waistcoat. She was very much frightened, and said, "01,' dear me, who ever is that ?" Prisoner was attempting to I uncover one of her daughters, who sleeps in the same room, when witness again asked " Who's that ?'' Prisoner re- plied "Me." Witness then raised an alarm, and awoke her I married daughter in the other room. A lodger was called, and prisoner went down stairs. A policeman having been infermed of the case, and a light obtained, the prieoner was found concealed between the pantry door and the wringing

Imachine, with his bead h.ld dowd behind the Inachine.— Inspector Wood : The two d tughters sleep in the same ' loom ? Yes.—Do you know this man at all ? 1 know him by sight P—Where does lie live? In Reline-lane.— Is he courting your daughter at all? No.—Prisoner : Flow could I get into the house when I was took in? When a man is drunk he cabal me and climb up the window; 1 am well aware of that.—Magistrate (to witness) : Were you there when he was found? Yes.-,—Did he appear to be drunk? He was pretending to be asleep; I don't know that he was drunk.—Have you ever spoken to him before? No. I know him by sight, and know his name.—Mrs. Taylor, daughter of last witness, corroborated the statement, and added that prisoner's coat and waistcoat were on the hearth- stone. She asked him what he was doing there, and bow he had got in, and be replied that he did not know. In answer to the magistrate witness saia the prisoner had " never crossed their doorstep before."--Barah Clarke, a good-look- ing young woman, said she did not see him when he pulled the bed clothes off her. She saw him down stairs, and identified him as one she knew by sight. She bad never spoken to him, and he was not courting her.— The magistrate: Did, he account how he had got in ?-11e said he didn't know.— Prisoner: I don't know how I got in.--P.C. Middlebrook said prisoner was sober when be-took him into custody, but be appeared to have had -some drink.—Prisoner : I don't know how I got into the house; it was a mystery to me when I found I was there. I was asleep when they came down to waken me. I had been up street, and had some drink. I had a good deal at Tom Mill's, in 13ridge-street. I was drunk when I left there.—The magistrate: Did you go anywhere else P-1 don't know; did I? (appealing to some one in court).—The young man questioned entered the box, and said he left prisoner drunk in the public-house in Bridge-street.—lnspector Wood said in April, 1877, prisoner was committed for trial on a charge of indecent assault, and sent to prison for three months.—The magistrate said: The case is a very suspicions one, and you say, as an excuse, that you didn't know what you were doing on account of your getting too much drink. This only shows what dis- graceful proceedings there are in St. Helens—people get their money and go and make themselves beastly drunk. Yen go to this house and frighten the people in it. It may have been much worse for you if the person living in the house had not disturbed you, and caused you to go away. You might have been standing in a much worse position than you do to-day. You will he fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. A GARDEN ROBBER CAUGHT.—Williarn Sefton (14) was charged with wilfully and maliciously damaging a plant, the property of Mr. David Gamble, Cowley Hill.—P.C. Smith shortly before seven o'clock that morning be saw the prisoner and two other boys in Cowley Hill-lane, and being suspicions of their movements, he concealed himself behind some bushes in a garden. One of the lads approached near to where he was concealed, but outside the garden, and after he had got 20 yards past, whistled to the other boys. The policeman then pulled off his hat in order to have a better view of the two lads standing near Mr. Gamble's garden; and he saw the prisoner enter the garden and pluck a geranium plant. He left his place of concealment and chased the prisoner down the lane, and caught him near Mr. Ansdell'e lodge. He had then the plant in his posses- sion.—John Slater, gardener r Mr. Gamble, said the geranium was worth from 6d. t d.; it would very likely mai fetch the latter sum in the et.—lnspector Wood said wilco the lad was brought to the office he sent for his parents, but they were not at home.—Prisoner, who had been previously convicted, was fined 6d. (damages) and Is and co* MOND ' efore F. W. Earle, Wm. Pilkington, and Wm:,, Blinkhorn. BREAING A MAN'S LEG.—Luke Malign, under remand charged with breaking the leg of a maY‘,named Taggart, near the Norton Arms, East-street, and who had been ad- mitted to bail, was again brought up.—Mr. Superintendent Johnston said the injured into %..ta .till in the Cottage Hospital, and unable to appear.—Pt isoner was remanded for another month, bail being allowed. BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Richard Foster and John Smith were summoned for committing a breach of the peace, by fighting together with their shirts off, on a waste piece of land on Cowley Hill, on July sth. Both defendants were bound over in their own recognisances of £lO, and one surety of £5 each, to keep the peace for three months.— Wm. Beck and Richard Jenkins were summoned for fighting together on Ormskirk-road, Rainford, on Tuesday last. Beck, who had five previous convictions recorded against him, was bound over in his own recognisance of £lO, and two sureties of £5 each, to keep the peace for three months, or 14 days' imprisonment; Jenkins in .£lO, and one surely of £5, or seven days' imprisonment. DEFAMATORY LA.NGUAGE.—Catberine Clark was sum- moned for using abusive language towards Ellen archibahl, in Critchley-street, on the 7th July.—Fined 2s. (3d. and costs, or seven days. NEGLECTING ins HORSE.—James Rhoden was summoned for being at such a distance from his horse and cart, in Elder-lane. Rainford, on the sth July, as to have no control over his horse.—Defendant said he had been into a field to purchase a cart, but he was not away long.—Mr. Earle: The pony might have run away.—llefendant : 1 know him too well for that. A pony 30 years at age would not run away. and I have had him 25 years.—Fined is. and 7s. GI costs

BREACH OF THE MINES REGULATION Acr.—Joseph Bur- rows was summoned for a breach of the Mines Regulation Act, by failing to sat props as soon as there was room, in his working at the Ashton F. Green Qollierv, on .the Ist July.— Mr. T. Swift appeared ter Messrs. Braman and Co., the colli?ry proprietors —Mr. Thomas Pennington said on (lie lst July he was going his round of the workings when he found defendant working underneath a head of coal, which was loose and broken, without sprags. Defendant first alleged he had no sprags but on witness finding one near lie said it was too short, but afterwards asked to be forgiven.— , Tbe Chairman said that as Messrs. Braman did not wish to I press the case heavily against the man he would only be fined lOs. and costs, or 10 days, but the Bench hoped it would be a warning to colliers to take greater care when at work.

A DISOBEDIENT APPRENTICE.—Joseph Kellett, an appren- tice at the glass works of Messrs. Pilkington was summoned for absenting himself from work and thereby disobeying an order made by the magistrates.—Mr. J. Swift said defendant had been away seven times since the order was made. On lone occasion he had gone to the works drunk and said he should oot work, and a policeman had to be sent for to eject him. That morning be said he should not appear.—Com- mitted to prison for 14 days with hard labour. KEEPING A BORROWED COAT.—George Lythgoe WAS charged with stealing a coat, value 35., the property of Jos. Fletcher, of Parr.—Mr. 'Superintendent Johnston stated the prisoner waa in the employ of prosecutor's father, as a farm labourer. On the 18th June prosecutor had lent pri- soner the coat, but he left the town and had not returned it. He was apprehended by Sergeant Whittaker in Bridge-street, when he was wearing the stolen article—Prisoner said he had had the coat several times, but had returned it. When he borrjwed it the last, time he got drunk, and found him- self in Wigan. When he became sober he was ashamed to come back. He had no intention of stealing ft.—The magistrates imposed a fine of 10s. and costs. or seven dealt' imprisonment with hard labour. STEALING A RICE PUDDING.—John Kelly, .1 youth of 16 years, was fined £1 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, for stealing a rice pudding from the eating house of Jno. Smith, in College-street, on Saturday night. TREFT OF FRUIT AND FLOWERS.—John Farrell, a middle aged man, who said he had been employed for 16 years by Colonel Gamble, was charged with stealing a quantity of fruit and flowers from the garden attached to Windle Cot- tage, the property of Colonel Gamble. P.C. Young caught prisoner As be was getting over the wall, and the fruit and flowers were found on him.—Fined 10s. and costs. or 14 days.

I TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Pilkington. ALLEGED THEFT OF GINGER BEER.—Patrick Kenney, a boy, was charged with stealing nine bottles of ginger boer, the property of Mr. William Smith, ginger beer manufacturer, of Parr —James Wood, a lad residing in College-staeet, and employed by Smith, said he was with a ginger beer cart in Pottery-street, Rccleston, on the previous forenoon. While getting a bill settled in a public house close by, he saw prisoner dismount the wheel of his cart, with either one or two bottles in his possession. On examin- ing the cart nine bottles were missing, and he went at once to Daulton's pottery through the gates of which he saw prisoner looking. He directly afterwards gave informatton to the police. He had known prisoner about twelve months by sight. —P.C. Robinson apprehended prisoner in Daul- tonN yard about twelve o'clock, charged him with stealing the bottles, but he made no reply, and commenced crying. He afterwards said a fellow labourer named McQueeney had given him a bottle and he did not know that it Was stolen. —Thomas McQueency, a lad, said hedid not give prisoner a bottle. Re did not see him after nine o'clock.—Prisoner Re gave it to another lad, and the other lad gave it to toe.— Remanded. THEFT OF OSTRICH FEATirmis.—Ann Burke, an elderly woman, was charged with stealing an ostrich feather ii-om Still in the market ground.—James Pickup, a draper, living at Blackburn, said he hold a stall on the St. Helens 31.‘rket Ground, which he attended to every Monday. He knew the prisoner by sight, as she had on several occasions inspected the goods upon his stall. On Monlay he missed two feathers, and he saw the prisoner walkaway from his stall to 'another. He did not see her take them as he was engaged at the other end of the stall, which is every long one. He followed the woman whom he asked what she had been taking front his stall, and she replied that she had not got any feathers of his in her possession. He lifted her shawl and found two underneath behind her shoulders. A crowd of people gathered round and d.sired him to let her go. jka he had his stall to attend to he allowed her to go on pay. ment of 55., which sum she offered to him. Soon after- wards he spoke to a policoman who apprehended her. Prisoner said she was reaching over a stall to point out i some article when the feathers stuck to her shawl.— I Remanded until Monday.

CAPTURE OF A MADMAN AT—RAINMILL.—EarIy on Thurs. day morning; a mail who gave the name of William Kelly, apparently a sailor, 29 years of age, was found wandering i about in a wild and naked condition, n Talbot's-lane. Rain- hill, by a gentleman. The police were communicated with, and P.C. Howarth took the man into custody. and conveyed him in a cab to Present police station, where he made several long rambling statements, one of which was to the effect that some one had shot and killed his wife, at Birkenhead on the previous night, but of course there was not a word of truth in it. As he appeared to be of unsound mind, he was detained, and on Thursday evening he was taken before Mr W. S. Evans, and Dr. Hall having seen the man, an order was made for his removal to Rainhill Alvin=

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND.

A Parliamentary return which his just been isued shows that, during the quarter ended June 30th,1,065 families were evicted in Ireland, 592 being re-admitted. Sums amounting to £1,700 have been awarded by the Grand Jury of tbe county of Limerick for malicious inju- ries of all sorts—cutting off of ears afid out of tongues of animals, Ac. • The Land League Convention, at which delegates attended from 26 branches in the counties of Down and Armagh, was held at Newry on Monday. The Rev. B. McKenna, c.c., of Kilcoo, asked what were 'they to do with merchants and shopkeepers who lead not come to their assistance.—A Voice: "Boycott them."— The Rev. Mr. McKenna: Oh, nonsense; but he would tell them what to do. Let any of them who had money spend it among their friends, and net give a single penny to those who were against them.—The Rev. Mr. O'Boyle, P.P., Saintfield, said he was of the people on whom Mr. Forster wished to let his hands foil; bet he defied hi.n. They were able to hold their own against the forces of Great Britain simply by not paying any atten- tion to them. The Irish agricultural statistics for 1881 are published as a Parliamentary paper. The number of Acres under 'crops was 5,121,833, showing a decrease against the previous year of 40,749. The number of holdings not exceeding one acre was 50,613, showing a slight increase. Every crop showed an increased average produce, that of turnips and potatoes being more than double compared with the previous year. At the weekly meeting of the Land League, in Dublin, on Tuesday, Mr. Sexton, M.P., presiding, the receipt was an—. flounced of £2.154 since last meeting. The Chairman made an appeal to the hotel owners and car owners cf Ireland, in defence of their roan business, to resent the attacks that were now being made upon their independence in the conduct of their private business, and to force them to entertain as guests men wbo were not only extremely objectionable to them, but whose presence in their hotels might inflict vital injury upon their business and endanger their friendly rela- tions with their neighbours. He called upon every man of them to start an independent fund to make hotel keepers and publicans who are despotised by the police and by the agents of the Urgency Committee to defend themselves in every part of Ireland. £5O were voted to assist the Scotch crofters who are 'fighting the land question on the coast of Scotland. , Twenty thousand Irishmen assembled in the Earl of Ran- forty's park, Dungannon, on Tuesday, when resolutions were passed condemning Home Rule and the land agitation, and thanking the Emergency Committee for their exertions. About 5,000 Orangemen met near Uewry, when resolutions were adopted repudiating :01 oymTathy with Cornmunisac agitators, and declaring a ti -1 determination to resist all attempts to disintegrate and orey the eitity of the British Empire. All passed off pear.... vat both meetings. Some rioting occurred in Netel on Tuesday night, and isolated individuals were beaten io the mob. The Catholics of Dunkinerly on Tuesday stoned the Orange procession passing through the streets. The Orangemen thereupon ~,.flred with revolvers, wounding a , policeman and a civilian. The latter is seriously in- ; pared. Constable William Bryan, of Portcullin, county Kil- kenny, while returning from Caetlewellan on a car, was stoned by a mob, and his helmet was kicked about the streets. A woman was also stabbed. A dreadful murder was committed on Tuesday night near Cappoquin, county Waterford, a woman named Grady haying her head severed from her body. A man named Thomas Buckley has been arrested. . Mr. Justice Lawson on Wednesday told a Kerry jury that trial by jury in that county was a sham, and expressed Ws belief that the present assizes would be the last at which a jury of Kerry men would have the opportunity of acquitting guilty persons. A gentleman who has just returned from visiting Mr. Michael Devitt, the founder and organiser of the National Land League, states that he is in excellent health, and spirits, and that he is perfectly satisfied with the treatment he is receiving, which is as considerate and kindly as the cir- cumstances permit. He is placed at no menial employment, and has every indulgence compatible with his position. A movement having been started among the public bodies in Ireland and Irish organisations in Great Britain to memorialise the Government for the release of the Rev. Eugene Sheaby, C.C., at present confined in Kilmainham as a "suspect," the rev, gentleman has written to his friends, *guesting them to discountenance any petition to the Crown or.to the Ministers of the Crown on the subject, and states that be asks for no favour, not given to his colleagues in detention. At the Tyrone assizes, which opened at Omagh on Wed- nesda:s, Mr. Justice Fitzgerald was presented with a pair of white kid gloves, there being no criminal cases for trial. Edmund O'Brien, farmer, and John Hyde, shopkeeper, both members of the Middleton Board of Guardians, were arrested on Wednesday under the Coercion Ad, and con- veyed to Limerick Gaol. • A party of men on Tuesday night entered the house of a man named Murphy, residing near Mill-street,•County Cork, and severely beat him. They also cut off qie tail of Mur- phy's horse, and made him swear to adhere to ate Land League.

div.head: ST. HELENS CHEMICAL CASK
div.p: A ST. HELENS CHEMICAL CASK

On Wednesday, at the St. Helens County Court, before Mr. Thompson, Thomas Anderton, caustic finisher, sought to recover £2 19s. 7d. from Messrs. Mcßryde and Co., chemical manufacturers.—Mr. Riley appeared for the plain- tiff, and Mr. Swift for the defendant company.—The defen- dants set up a counter claim for £5 in respect of damages sustained by plaintiff's negligence and want of care.—Mr. Riley said the claim of £2 19s. 7d. was made up thus: £1 Bs. ld. wages actually earned, and £1 us. ed., being an average weekly wage in lieu of notice. On Thursday, the 7th April. plaintiff was wrongfully dismissed by the defen- ,dants, and up to that time had actually earned the amount mentioned. Also, according to the custom and usage, he was entitled to a week's notice before this dismissal, and £1 11. ed. was fixed for it. His case was that on the'day be- fore the 7th—Wednesday—he was instructed by the manager of the works to fill 100 drums of caustic out of a particular pot. He was told there would not be quite enough stuff to fill the drums, and was instructed to leave the drums three or four inches short of being full, so that if there was any more caustic left In the pot he could go over them again. The plaintiff's duty in the matter was ladling the caustic out of the pot into a "ehoqt " which was conveyed by this means into the hundred drums attended to, by what was called a middleman, who was liable for the way in which the drums were filled. Plaintiff would swear that he informed the " middleman," whose name was George Murphy, of the instructions he had re- ceived, and from time to time went to see how he was I getting on. Ho (Mr. Riley) believed it was the case that about three or four were only half full.—Plaintiff said lie lived in Grant-street, and had worked a year and nine months at his present place. He had previously worked 1 two years at the same place. He had had ten years expe- rience as a caustic finisher, and had been all his life about chemical works. He informed Murphy of the instructions be had recieved, and reminded him about a dozen times during the progress of the work. The bottoms of the pot he packed into the two drums. Mr. Blinkhorn, the managing director, said the packing had been done very unevenly, to which he (witness) replied that he could not see he was to blame at all, as he had repeatedly spoken to the middle- man about exercising great care in packing. Murphy was then brought up, and he admitted that he had been told. He exercised great care in the " baling " out of the liquid, and he was told by Mr. Riley, Mr. Blinkhorn's deputy, that ihe caustic was in good condition for being packed. Mr. Blinkhorn sub- sequently said he was sick of the lob and ordered plaintiff to put on his coat and go home.—John Day, foreman at Messrs. Kurtz' works, said it was a foreman's duty at places where he had worked to say when the caustic was ready for packing.—James McNab, formerly a caustic finisher, said it was physically impossible for the man " baling " out the liquid to superintend its running into , the drums, and it was also impossible to prevent a portion of the " bottoms " running along with the pure liquid.— For the defence it was contended that plaintiff bad not I exercised sufficient care in sending the liquid down the shoot, and the result WAR that forty drums were lost. The loss they assessed at £5. A sample of good caustie soda was produced and contrasted with "an average sample " of one of the forty drums of caustic. The latter one was much darker than the former.—A verdict was given for the plaintiff for £1 Ss. id, and a verdict on defendant's set off, the costs to follow each event.

ZION CHAPEL SUNDAY SCHOOL, PRESCOT.—The annual treat to the scholars attending the above school was held On Monday, in the park belonging to the late Sir T. B. Birch. At one o'clock the scholars, to the number of about 180, met at the school, and, having formed into procession, headed by the band of the 2nd L.E.V., marched to the park. On the way several stoppages were made, and hymns sung by the children. Various games were indulged in by the scholars, and a large number of races were run for small prizes. During the afternoon, selections of music were discoursed by the band. At four o'clock the children sat down to an excellent tea and at five o'clock tea was provided for the visitors, of wlom there were abut a hundred. At half-past eight the children reformed into procession, when Mr. Jas p.nluudill proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. l'anter, for hi ici " s d,p933 in granting the use of the park. Before leaving thec,iteea.lo the scholars each received a supply of nuts and

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

An inquest was opened on the body of the murdered woman, on Wednesday afternoon, at the house of Mr. Tickle Red Lion Hotel, Parr, by Mr. Barker, deputy coroner. A large crowd of people assembled outside the public-house. The jury was composed of the following gentlemen : Messrs. W. G. Marsh, James Bennett, George Barton, Geo. Pennington, Henry Martin, Jesse Boydell, Thomas West, John Sutton, John Huyton, John Green, Peter Tickle, Mat- thias Bailey, and James Lewis.

Mr. Barker said be was very sorry that they bad to I assemble together that day to inquire into the cause of the death of this unfortunate woman, whose datlll appeared to , have been attended with very brutal violemerto The enquiry was very important, and at the conclusion they would have to say whether the apprehended man was responsible for her death, and if so whether he was guilty of murder or of manslaughter. Under one of these terms he must of necessity be guilty, but upon the evidence he would have something to say subsequently, and upon the distinction between the two verdicts. If they come to the conclusion that the death was the result of violence given to an healthy woman, it would be a question as to whether the , verdict was one of murder or not. He understood she was a delicate woman, and if her death had been accelerated by violence, then the verdict would be one of manslaughter. The deceased woman and the man in custody lived with the parents of the deceased woman at their house in Barber- street. He went to his work on Monday and came home in the evening, washed himself, and went out to assist his sister-in-law in removing 1 some furniture; and came home in the evening about twelve I and murdered his wife. It appeared the unfortunate woman was in bed, and he called to her to get up to get him some supper, although she was in delicate health at the time. He followed her downstairs, in fact went down in such a manner that the old man thought lie was break- ing the stairs down, and they remained downstairs about ten minutes. The deceased woman then went up- stairs and sought protection, complaining yery much of pain in her head occasioned by the violence ef her husband. The man followed her up and made use of languace he did not like to repeat and suiting the action to the word struck her with his clenched fiat on the head. The father and mother jumped out of bed and endeavoured to prevent any further violence, but before they could do this he gave his wife another blow and felled her. The mother, told him to go about his business, and the father went and attended to I the poor woman. It appeared they had not lived together happily for several years. After he had knocked the woman down he told her that unless she got up he would kick her ribs out. It was a matter whether that was intended. He simply proposed to open the enquiry and -then Adjourn it to some future day for the convenience of the jury and police. They would take the evidence of the mother and then give an order for the interment and for the post mortem examination. 1 The jury then went and viewed the body, and on their return. 1 Margaret Murphy, wife of Owen Murphy, residing at 19, Barber-street, Parr, said: Edward Foy is my son-in-law; he married my daughter Bridget about four years ago. They lived in a house by themselves for a few months, and then came to live with me in Barber-street. The prisoner some- times went away and remained away for months at a time 1 at places unknown, and he and his wife have lived very un- happy together. They quarrelled and he struck her in my presence about a week previous to my daughter's death. She complained of weakness and was attended by Dr. Donnellan, who visited her twice. On Sunday evening last the 10th inst. deceased dressed and told the prisoner that she was going to see the doctor. He then swore and said if she went he would I kick her ribs out. She did not go. On Monday be went to his work at Messrs. Kuitz's Chemical Works, and in the evening came home, and after cleaning himself and , eating his meal went out to his sister-in-law's house in 1 Atlas-street to help to remove their furniture. He came back about eleven o'clock in the evening. We had all gone ' to bed. I and my husband were in the front room, and had prisoner's eldest girl, three years old. with us. His wife and youngest child, twelve months old, were in bed. I beard him go into his wife's room. He swore and said, "Get up, and get me my supper, or I will pull you out of bed." I heard a noise as if he had pulled her out. She went down stairs, and he followed. I could hear him call- ing and Cursing her. She then came into the room where I and my husband were. She stood over main bed, ar.d im- mediately afterwards he came into the room and said, " to your soul ; come out of that," at the same time raising his hand and striking baron the head. I then jumped out of bed and got between them. He said, "Oh you—" raised his fist and struck her a severe blow on the bead, and she fell on the floor, and never spoke after- wards. She groaned once and died almost im- msdiately. I told him that he had killed her, and he said "If she doesn't get up out of that I will kick her ribs?! He then went downstairs, and I again told him she 1 was dead. He asked for his cap. which I threw at him, and 1 be went away. That was about twelve o'clock midnight. I did not see him again until ten o'clock on the morning of ' Wednesday, when I saw bins in the police court. Prisoner I was fond of a glass of ale. He was jealous of her, but had I no Cause.
The Coroner: Have you anything /0 add to that state- ment ? - - -
Wine: I hare nothitM to add. and nothing to take from it. _ . _

Owen Murphy, father of the deceased. said : I reside at 19, Barber-street, Parr. The prisoner and his wife have lived with me since they were married with the exception of a few months when they lived in a house by themselves.' Prisoner went away, leaving his wife and children with me for months at a time. One time be stayed away about eight or nine months, and I had to keep his wife and chil- dren. They have never lived comfortably together. Ho often struck her. For a week previous to her death she complained of weakness and was attended by Dr. Donnellan. She wanted to go out to see the doctor o), Sunday last, but prisoner would not allow her, and be sail he would kick her ribs out D he went. She did not gc.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: ST. HELENS TOWN COUNCIL

A LTII COMMITTEE. The meiii4ers ‘.I this co.mniuee held a meeting on Wed- nesday, when there were present Messrs. Twyford (chair- man) Fisher, McKechnie, Brooke, Wilcock, Foster, Brewis (town clerk), McNicoll (medical officer), and Hart (sur- veyor),

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER.
A communication was read from the Local Goverumeist Board sanctioning the re-appointmeut of Dr. McNicll as medical officer for the borough at a salary of t 200 per annym.

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that there had been 257 births during the month, and 92 deaths, representing .a death-rate of 16-21 per 1,000, corresponding rate last year 1935. Samples of water had been taken by Inspecte Williams front that portion of the brook called Eccleston brook, from the usual place, viz., Spray's bridge, Liverpool-road, near the timber yard, by Messrs. Wash's works, and by Messrs. Lyon's honk, works. No acid was found in any of these, but a faint add in one sample from the drain belonging to the Bridgewater works, but not of sufficient strength to affect the brook. A sample from Greenbankl alkali works draining into Potte street is full of sulphur thrown out by strong aoid and givi off sulphuretted hydrogen very freely. The canal also, Greenbank, was strongly acid in a sample taken June 2 rd. Samples taken from Harlshaw brook at the gas works yard, from Mr. Kurtz's works, and the Metal Extracting Works drains, are nearly free altogether from acid,:and the drain- age from the St. Helens chemical works is being neutralised by lime. Id consequence of this, the smell of sulphuretted hydrogen in Warrington Nestroad for the last month has greatly diminished. The overflow water from the canal at Merton Bank Bridge, and from the drain at the Globe alkalfi works, are both strongly acid. Glover-street is still infested with bad smells, and requires a ventilating shaft to be carried from the sewer to a height above the houses. Inspector Houghton has called my attention to the state of a house ia No. 3 court, Parr-street. There is a rent throus,h the house which not only lets in the rain, but threatens to bring the gable end to the ground. The house is tenanted by Catherine McFarlane. The next house is inhabited by John Power, and is bad also. Three houses in Peasley Cross-lane are in like condition to the last named. A rift runs from top to bottom, and lets in both wind and rain. The roofs are very defective. Inspector Houghton took me to a house in Manner-street, which is also rents. through, and seems ready to part company with its neigh- bours. The windows will not open, and the rain pours in. It appears as if all these houses were undermined. They must be repaired or closed. The health of the town is in a satisfactory state.—The subject of the state of the houses in Parr-street and Riinmer-street was referred to the next meeting.

• UNITED METHODIST Fans CHURCH SCHoOL, PEES- COT.—On Monday the scholars attendim: the United Metho. that Free Church Sunday School, Victoria-place, Prescot, had their annual treat in Knowsley Paik. At half-past on. o'clock aboa seventy scholars put in appearance at the school. A procession was then formed, and headed by the Rev. Mr. Bishop, the pastor, marched to the park. where the children dispersed and proceeded to amuse themselvem as they thought proper. Tea was partaken of, and on the scholars reaching the schools, after leaving the park, nuts and cakes were given to them.

div.p: TR 14, R7i_Alll-Nll, SATURDAY, JULY 16, 1881.

"nothing so much, prevents the spread of improve- r ment and the attempts of enterprise, as that the industries of the country should be fettered by un- necessary legislation," he straightway assails those economists and capitalists (including men of different politics), who have argued that legislation in such directions as the compulsory reduction of the hours of labour may be overdone.. Lord Bandon exclaims : "When they say your commercial greatness depends upon having cheap labour, that cheap labour means low wages, and low 'wages means uncomfortable homes," &c., &c. Then' we are to understand that ; Lord Bandon has changed his tune, and that, in spite of his own sage axiom, the fettering of the country's industries by legislation is a right course, and does : not prevent improvement and the "attempts of enterprise." Is that it ? L frd Bandon, as we have seen before by his conduct in the House, has sugar bounties on the brain. Again at Latham he harps upon them, and declares that "the great staple industries of England" are being "gradually, starved and ruined by the system of foreign bounties." We are curious to see what Lord Bandon will proceed to argue from that premise, be it true or not. He has I nothing to recommend beyond this, that "every Government which has the welfare of the country at stake, should watch the duties which foreigners put upon English goods, so as to see that Englishmen are not receiving unfair play in the commercial slruggle of the world." Is it imaginable, then, that any Government of ours has not." watched "the duties foreigners have put goon English goods? We have ample evidence that the present Government has kept its eye sharply upon the attempts of other countries to obstruct our trade with them by protective duties, and even now this Government is doing its utmost in a treaty with- France and Spain to obtain more equitable terms of commercial intercourse between this country and them. But no British Government, however watchiul, can prevent foreign governments from imposing import duties if they so resolve. The late Conservative Government, which had the benefit of Lord Sandon's shining talents and sapient counsels, being one which "had the welfare of the country at stake," no doubt did "watch the .duties foreigners put upon English goods." But watching was all. We have not heard of anything that the Beaconsfield Government did, or tried to do, to stop foreigners from levying such duties. Possibly Lord Sandon thinks a Liberal Government can dq, and ought to do, what a Tory Government can't accomplish. We believe it can do so, and will in many a useful measure of administration and legislation. But we trust and believe a Liberal Government will never be the first to adopt a false and ruinous fiscal policy of retaliatory protection, sue& as Lord Bandon is driving at. If that fatal step is to be taken some day, let it be by a Tory Government, and let it bear the respon- sibility of the consequences. •

I A sad rumonr is in circnbtion illustrative of the sympathy said to exist between beer and Conservatism. Some time ago a certain branch of a Conservative Associa- tion resolved to change their quarters from the temple of Bacchus, in which they had been wont to assemble, to an establishment wheria nothing stronger than the mild Beim-. biting beverages ofiChina and Mocha was obtainable. Sad to say, however, no sooner had the change been effected than a change for the worst appeared amongst the members, as their interests in the cause waned very quickly. Meetings became more and more thinly attended and even committee men dropped off/ one by one. The pitch of enthusiasm which it was desirable should exist amongst the members of the association could not, somehow, be attained at a coffee shop. At length it was decided that there were grounds-- presumedly coffee grounds—for returning .to their old quarters and I learn that since .taking this step the associa- tion has grown considerably stronger. FLACCUS.

BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION COMPA.NY'S EXCURSION FROM RUNCORN.—On Saturday, the employes of the Bridge- water Navigation Company at Runcorn, had their annual excursion to Liverpool in one of the Company's steamers. HOLY TRINITY DAY Scaoms, RusconiN.—:On 'Sun- day, the annual sermons on behalf of these schools were preached by the Rev. T. Meadows, vicar of Thornton, and late of Runcorn. The 'collections scarcely amounted to as much as last year. THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.—The following appoint- ments for this district have been made by the Stationing Committee :—Runcorn, Rev. George Hack; Widnes, Rev. H. Needle; St-Helens, Rev. Jahn M. Walmaley. THE PRIMITIVE METHODISTS AT RUNCORN.—The new superintendent minister' of the Preston Brook Circuit, the Rev. J. Pickw€ll, will preach two sermons in the Greenway- road Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday, on the occasion of the chapel anniversary. On Monday night a tea and reception meeting will be held: FLOWER SERVICE AT BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUNCORN.—On Sunday night, a flower service will be held at .Bethesda Chapel, Runcorn. The building will be decorated with flowers, the sermon will be preached by the Rev. J. D. rhomas, and each member of the congregation will be expected to wear "a buttonhole." PROMENADE MUSIC AT WIDNES. —On Monday even- ing the Star of Temperance brass band played the following programme on the promenade .at Widnes :—Overture, "Confidence*" (J. Hemmerle) • selection, "Notre Chere Alsace" (H. Kling) ; quadrille, "Olivette " (H. Kling); selection, " Pride of Scotland" (51. Round); vain, "True love " (11. Round) : polka, "Bijou " (Metcalfe); fantasia, "11 Trovatore " (Verdi); schottische, "The signal" (M. Seaman) ; National Anthem. • Sours KENSINGTON ExeacrwaTioxs.—The following students were successful at the examination of the Runcorn Mechanics' Institute held in May last. First-class element- ary and Queen's prizes, J. G. Hinton, T. Simpkin, and W Millington. Second-class, J. M. Frith and G. G. Tomlinson. W. Millington obtained tke first prize at the Sessional Ex- aminations, and T. Simpkin the second prize. ROBBERY AT Wirer Es. —At the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Wednesday, George Radford, aged 31, labourer, was' sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment for having, at Widnes, on the 23rd November, 1879, stolen two boxes of caper tea, the property of Ellen Ellwood and others, for having, on the 28th July, 1880, stolen a clock, the property of Edmund Louies, and for having, on the 24th July, 1880, stolen two woollen shirts, the property of John Noon. WIDNES Sawn TER.—The scholars and friends connected with the Widnes Parish Church Sunday Schools, Waterloo-road and Simms-cross, had their annual treat on the Bth inst. About 1,000 scholars assembled at the Waterloo-road School-room at one o'clock, and were marshalled into a procession. They then walked t 5 the Central railway station where a special train was in waiting to convey them • to Helewood, where the afternoon was agreeably spent is a field kindly lent by Mr. Twiggs. The young people were also entertained at tea. RUNCORN Srman•Bowswrr SOCIETY.—It will be seen from an advertisement in our columns that over £20,000 worth of shares have already been issued in this society (the 406th). The first subscription night is on 'Monday, the 25th inat., and the first appropriat;on on Molday, the 31st August, in the Public Hall, when Mr. Starr, or his agent, will attend. All who become members on or before the 31st August will be qualified to participate in the appropriation. The society in Wigan has already had several appropriations and appears to be making rapid progress. At a late meeting ! the winner of the appropriation proved to be a member who bad only joined that very night, which very naturally caused a little chagrin on the part of the others. A resolution was ; passed that members who had only joined the same evening as the appropriation was made should not be allowed to par- , ticipate.

• T}lo Town Connell on Wednesday had a discussion ett tia• Tre.t.4azy ottirr tor the payment of the • sum of £3,352, the costs of the inquiry into the corrupt • election practices. One of the aldermen said it was a hard- ship that women ratepayers, who had not the Parliamentary franchise. ehould have to pay the rate rendered necessary by the political sins of the city. PLEUEO- PNEUMONIA AND POCT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE. —The Clerk of the Pelee on Saturday, received information that this disease had re-appeared on the farm of John Coar, Yew Tree Farm, Livesey, near Blackburn. One cow was attacked, and this has, by order of the local authority, been slaughtered. Another animal belonging to Edward Shor- rock, Brook Farm, Ramsgreave, near Blackburn, suffering from the same disease, has been slaughtered. Foot-and: mouth dieettse is rapidly dying out in the county, only one fresh outbreak having been reported since June 21st. There are now only 30 farms infected in Lancashire, being a diminution of 25 since the 18th of last month. A ST. HELENS MAN KILLED AT LITERPOOL.—An inquest was held on Tuesday by Mr. Clarke Aspinall, coroner, on the body of Thomas Kirby, twent'y-eight years of age, a black- smith who lived at 10, New Cross-street, St. Helens. De- ceased, who had been working for his brother in Liverpool, was found injured in Lime-street Station shortly after midnight on Friday. A parcel van had been shunted down the " Booth " siding, and when it came along No. 1 platform a shout was heard, and, ca searching, deceased was discovered lying under the overhanging platform, with one leg across the rail. His leg was so severely injured that, on his arrival at the Royal Infirmary, it was amputated, but he died on Saturday morning from the shock. There was no evidence to show how the deceased got under the van. The last time he was seen alive was between nine and ten o'clock on Thursday night, wl.en he called on a person in Nerth- ampton-street for the loan of some money to pie his fat e to St. Helens. He was quite sober at the time. Tne jury re- turned a verdict to the effect that heath was due to shock consequent upon the injury to his leg, caused by being run over by a parcel van which was being shpnted down a sid- ing at Lime-street Station, but how the deceased got upon the line there was no evidence to show. SOUTHPORT AND WEST LANCASHIRE BANKING COM • rANY (LIMITED).—The lnvesters' Guardian gives the fol- lowing in its list of new companies :—This is the reconstruc- tion of an existing company of the same name. It was registered on the Ist inst., with a capital of £440,000, in £5 shares, of which 50,000 are preference shares. The new company will take over the liabilities of the old, and will allot one ordinary share in respect of each share in the old company, but no sum of money shall be deemed to have been paid up on such shares. The new company is to open a separate account, and to the credit of the same is to place £20,000 as the value of the bank premises and furniture at' Southport, Ormskirk, and elsewhere, belonging to the old company. The subscribers are—" *Samuel Boothroyd, J.P., Southport, 1,000 shares; *Walter Smith, J.P., Southport, 1,000; B. Cheesham, Southport, 100; *John Untrin, South- port, 100; *R. Nicholson, J.P., Southport. 150; E. Eldon. Southport, bootmaker, 200; T. Fisher. Southport, confec- tioner, 50. The number of directors is not to be less than 7, nor more than 11; qualification, 400 shares, or £2,000 stock. , The first are Messrs. Hugh Ainscough, J. Kay, William Sharp, J. Thorley, T. M. Williamson, Edward Chatres Mad- dison, and the subscribers denoted by an asterisk. The company in general meeting will determine the remunera- tion.

Mu= To AN ELoPEsemr.—At the Bolton Quarter Ses- sions on Tuesday, William Kenyon, 'agent, Blacldourn, wa4 charged with stealing a recipe book and two boxes of cigars, the prcperty of Alice Scholes. The prosecutrix for- merly kept a confectioner's shop in Blackburn, where she made the acquaintance of the prisoner. According to her statemeot, he represented himself as single, and induced her to elope with him to Bolton where they furnished a house. Subsequently, Mr. Richard Scholes, member of a local board, and cousin of the prosecutrix, discovered that prisoner was married, and told him he had better get back to his family at Blackburn. The prisoner went, taking with him the articles mentioned in the indictment. Since his committal he has written to the prosecutrix, threatening her that if she allows the case to proceed he would bring witnesses`, who would swear she knew all along he was married. The prisoner denied having placed the cigars in his trunk, and said the prosecution had been instigated by Mr. Scholes, because the latter had been summoned for having by threats compelled him (Kenyon) to sign over the furniture to the. young woman.—The deputy recorder justified Scholes, say- ing many men would have horsewhipped the prisoner, whom he sentenced to twelve months' hard labour.' The statistics just issued by the Committee of Coun- cil on Education afford some interesting and instruc- tive particulars with regard to the work of the Edu- cation Act in England and Wales. We are told that the principal work of the past year has been to com- plete the universal enforcement of school attendance by compulsory laws. About 6,000,4200 persons have been brought under these laws in 1880, and within Et few weeks of the 27th of June direct compulsion will be the law enforced upon all children between the ages of five and thirteen. It appears, however, that the necessity oi compulsory attendance at school is still great. Whilst the voluntary schools pro- vide accemmodation for 3,000,000, there are less than 2,000,000 in average attendance. Board schools have accommodation for i,000,000, and there are about three•quarters of a million in attendance daily. If the schools were properly distributed, the accom- modation would be sufficient, but then the population is migratory, so that whilst boards have to erect new schools in large towns, there is more room than can be utilised in small places. For every 100 seats in board schools the average attendance is about 71, and in voluntary schools 63. Whilst of those on the books in board schools the attendance is 70•84 per cent, and in voluntary wheels 70.52. It is thus patent that it is much easier to induce children to become scholars than to ensure their regular attend- ance. Strong complaints are made in the report that the education of so many chileren of to years and upwards is discontinued, as soon as by passing the fourth standard, they are released from the compulsory laws. Nearly roo,ooo out of a total of 231,483 examined in the fourth standard last year left school to go to work, and the committee urge that an amendment of the act relating to this subject is muoh needed. The report shows that the position of clenuntary teachers has improved very considerably of late years. The average salary of certificated mas- ters has increased from £96 to £l2l since 1870, and 'hat of certificated mistresses from £57 to £72. The report as a whole is of a very satisfactory character, tending to show that the educational department of the country is being looked after as carefully, and is making as much progress, as its great importance demands.

This (Friday) morning the prisoner was brought befora Mr. Blinkhorn, magistrate,•at the Town Hall, and charged, on remand, with causing the death of his wife. Mr. Johnston, superintendent of po!ice, said Foy had alreidy been brought up, upon the charge, and be should be glad if the magistrate would remand him until Saturday, when the adjourned inquest would probably have ter- minated. •
Mr. Blinkhorn accordingly remanded the prisoner until to-morrow (Saturday).

The adjourned inquest was held this day, at a quarter past eleven o'clock, in the witness room adjoining the police court, before Mr. T. W. Barker, deputy coroner. Prisoner was accommodated with a seat at the end of the coroner's table, and there were also present: Mr. Supt. Johnston, P.C. Lain,lVidnes, who captured the prisoner, and P.C. Sheriff. The prisoner appeared quite calm in his demeanour.

The Coroner said that when the jury met the other day, they would remember that the evidence of the 'father and mother of the deceased was taken. On that occasion the priaoner was not before them; and what he (Mr. Barker) proposed to do that day was to read over that evidence in the presence of Foy, which would give the jury the oppor- tunity of putting any further questions, and the prisoner the chance of asking anything:, or making any statement he might choose. After doing this, they would take the further evidence which had to be brought before them by the super- intendent of police. He did not think the enquiry would take them very long. I the evidence of Mrs. Murphy Was then read over,.and, in answer to further questions from the Coroner, witness said she did not think deceased was more than 24 years of age. ; The Superintendent remarked that he had understood I sha was about 34 years old; but he could not vouch for the accuracy of this information, as his opinion was based upon the particulars ziven to him by the police-constable who had enquired into the matter. In reply to further questions, Mrs. Murphy said the prisoner frequently struck his wife, and she believed he had always been jealous of her. Foy was In the habit of taking . considerable drink, and it was chiefly on these occasions that he was violent to hie wife. A Juryman: Was there a light in the room when she came in ?
