Witness: Yes, yes, I did ; it was a hard sight. Coroner (to prisoner) : Now you can ask any question upon what she has said. Did you hear when I read it over; did you hear what I said just now? Prisoner: Well, I didn't take any notice. Coroner: Ah, well that's your fault, not mine. Do you want to put any question to her? Prisoner: When I came home that night I wanted her to take off her clothes. Coroner: Don't make any statement; just ask a question. IF you don't want to ask her it is quite right. Prisoner then said something, when he was told he could make a statement afterwards. _ _ . .
-- The evi !enee of Owen Murphy, labourer, Barber-street, Parr, was next read over, and the prisoner listened attentively to it.

Witness, on coming to that part of the evidence where he stated he had not seen the prisoner since, appeared mach moved on seeing the prisoner at the other end of the table. Ho said (raising his hand) Ah ! I see you there now; and began' to weep. The Coroner : You can put any question you like to the witness.

The Prisoner : Where were you when I came home from my work in the evening? Superi ntenden t Johnston: Now that is a fair question. Witness: I and my wife were in bed, and my daughter and her child were in bed, too. • The Coroner: Did you mean the first time at five o'clock?

Prisoner: Yes, when I came home first. Witness : I was in the house, sir, sitting by the fire. Mr. Johnston (to prisoner): Any other question? Prisoner (sotto voce): I don't like to ask any question. A Juryman: ,We wish to know if there was light enough to enable them to see him strike her; and what be struck her with. Witness : He struck her with his shut fist.

Patrick Kiernan a lodger with the prisoner, was then sworn, and said that Foy used to talk as if he were jealous of his wife, but he could not say whether that was the real 1 cause of their quarrelling. In reply to the question whether the deceased was a quarrelsome woman, witness said that he did not observe that she j was so except in the case of her husband. ' In answer to the question as to whether he had heard the prisoner use any threat to the woman, be replied that he had heard Foy say" he would rule her," and " make her do what she ought." The Deputy Co-oner : Well, that is very proper. A husband ought to rule his wife, but I suppose the practicil experience is that the wife generally rulee! Witness (proceeding) said it would be about eleven o'clock when the prisoner come borne on the night of the alleged murder. He mild not say whether Foy was "drunk "at the time. He (prisoner) appeared to hive had something to drink, but he knew what .he was about. At the time when the prisoner returned, he (witness) was upstairs in the bed room where lie usually slept. He heard Fay go into the back room where his wife slept. When he went into the room he told her to get out of bed and make it again, and he also said that he wanted supper. Subsequently be told her if she did not get up he would pull her out of bed. He was quite sure be heard that, as his room was close to the one in which deceased slept. He believed she said in reply, "Let me alone." The prienner and deceased then went dawn attire. Before that he did not hear a noise of violence. He heard a moving of clothing as it deceased were getting out of bed. He believed she went downstairs first. He did not hear, any unusual noise down- stairs. Fey and his wife spoke to each other sharply, and remained downstairs not more than four or five minutes. Deceased came up first and went into her father's bedroom, where hi) (witness) was also in bed. She asked if they were all there, and complained that her husband had knocked her head against the wall. Prisoner at this time had either entered the room or was ascending the stairs. He believed prisoner would heir what the woman said. Prisoner told deceased again to make his bed, but she refused. Ho then struck her a slight stroke.

The Coroner to witness: Now you must speak the whole truth; you must not mind the fact of the prisoner being be- foie you. Witness: Oh, yes, I will tell the whole truth. . Witness then went on to say that deceased was standing at the time the prisoner struck her. Foy then gave her another blow. The Coroner: Was this a small blow.

Witness: Well, it was the blow that confirmed her death. Witness proceeded to say that deceased did not speak and he assisted deceased's father and mother in lifting her 'up. Prisoner then left the house.
A jaryman: Was she a temperate woman? Did she get drink ?
Witness: I can't exactly say what they might drink when I was not looking at them.

Cormier : But —did you ever see her in drink? Witness: She might have been what you would call "half In drink." He had occasionally seen the deceased in a public-house, taking a glass, but had not noticed her sitting In such place as if she was on a drinking bout. He could not say whether de.:eased was drunk or sober at the time she was killed.
The Coroner (to witness): Would you have called her a drunken woman
Witness: I would not like to call any woman a drunken woman, or any man a drunken man. (Laughter.) The Coroner: What I mean. is, was she an habitual drinker?
Witness: Well, I could not be there to see what be did, master, because I used to be away; I could net afford to spend my time in the house.
•Mr. Barker : Then you do not consider she was a drunken woman ? •

Witness: Some might call her so. By a Juryman: Have you ever seen her making very free with other men than her husband in public-houses Witness : No. She might have some little joke with a man, the same as her class of people will do, but no more. Another Juryman: Did you ever see them fighting? Witness: Sometimes she would fight as hard as he would fight. That is true. At other times the , prisoner and deceased would be great friends. . . . .

Prisoner (interrupting—) : She was drunk at dinner time,. and at six o'clock in the evening, and on seeing her BO I walked out of the house. (To witness.) Didn't you carry her beer to get drunk? Witness : When?
Prisoner : Why, many a score of times. Did you see her drunk during la 4 week? . _ _
Witness : I could not swear, nor could I say how many imes I have seen her disorderly.

- The Superintendent of Police: The witness asks you how many times his wife was drunk during the past Month, and you say that you don't know. Then the pris net ealck "Was she drunk ten times during the past month."
Prisoner (Interrupting and addressing the w—ilness): 'Now don't tell a lie.

At this stage, the juty adjourned for 40 minutes for lun- cheon. On retnrning, Bose Kelly, 14, Barber-street, was called, and said she formerly lived at the house of the prisoner, and left there about six weeks ago. Prisoner and his wide were then in the habit uf quarrelling every Saturday night, when he was generally drunk. Prisoner was a jealous-minded fellow. She had every reason to believe that the deceased was a respectable woman. Prisoner was continually snarling at his wife, and had threatened to kick her ribs out if she did not give up drinking. Deceased took drink, and she had seen her drunk. ' ' Patrick Donnellan, physician and surgeon, St. Helens, said he made the post mortent examination of deceased on Wednesday. Externally there was one mark of violence, which was over the region of the liver. A blow or a fall might produce the mark. If she had fallen against a hard substance the mark might have beeu caused. The brain was slightly congealed. There were two clots of blood in the two laterial ventricles about the size of a pea. The brain was unusually firm in- dicating that she had been taking drink. 7.'he heart was flabby and weak, and the lungs were congested, apparently the effects of drink. The liver was enlarged. ' The kidneys were very much congested and fatty, and the stomach also. All the internal organs indicated that the doceased had been In the habit of tatting too much drink. The cause of death was the weakness of the body not allowing the system to recover itself; and a shock or blow acting upon A weak and diseased system would cause death. The Coroner: Supposing there had been no shock to the system she might have lived for some time. Witness : Oh, yes. The Coroner: Some years, perhaps? • Witness: possibly; I don't think very probably. The Coroner: Just within the range of possibility ? Witness Yes. The Coroner: Supposing ho struck her in the bed-room , and she fell against the wall, would that be likely to cause death. .

Witness : No, she must have fallen against something pointed, and upon that particular spot I have mentioned. The Coroner: Suppose she had fallen against some article of furniture woulel that be likely to have caused death?
Witness: Yes. • The Coroner: Would the blow on the head produce the clots of blood?

Witness : I think so, considering the system. The blow given ro a healthy person would not in my opinion cause death. But the peculiarity of these drinking people is this: the 'blood vessels of the brain are not elastic. In the

case of a drunkard they are inelastic. The blow on the head as described would probably produce the clots. The Coroner: Supposing there had not been this fall or kick in the region of _the. Jiver—would that blow alone and

the state of the brain be likely to cause death. Witness: Ido not think the clots would be much; they would not contribute much to the death of the person. The cause of death was, no doubt, the sudden shock to the system. The Coroner : Have you attended the deceased? Witness: I have attended per for weakness and general debility, and the symptoms she then exhibited bear out what is proved by the examination of the body. The post- mortens examination showed exactly what I expected to fwd. I attended her the week previous. The Coroner: Supposing nothing at all had been done to the deceased, how long do you think she would have lived? Witness: It would depend entirely upon the amount she drank. (Laughter.) P.C. George Laing, Widnes,deposed that be apprehended the prisoner on Tuesday night, at half-past nine. He told him he should have to take him to St. Helens on a charge of murdering his wife on the previous Monday night, at eleven o'clock. Prisoner replied, " I no more killed her than what you did." He brought the prisoner to St. Helens and gave him into the custody of Superintendent Johnston. The Coroner then summed up at considerable length, and directed the jury as to the points of law involved in the case.
The jury were dismissed to another room to consider their verdict, but they only absented themselves about two minutes.

The Coroner : Gentlemen of the jury, have you agreed upon your verdict? • The Foreman: We have. The Coroner: What verdict do you find? The Foreman: Manslaughter. The prisoner was then formally committed for trial at the Liverpool Assizes on the charge of manslaughter ; and the Proceedings terminated.

DENOUEMENT OP AN ELOPMENT.—At Accrington, on Monday, Peter Whittaker, late assistant market inspector, was charged by the relieving officers at Accrington with neglecting to maintain his wife. A few weeks ago the prisoner eloped with dnother man's wik leaving hh, own wife without any moans, anti be was discovered living at Bury with his inamorata. Hb seas committed to prison for fourteen days, withliberty to settle.

opened on Thursday. Chief Justice Lord Coleridge, who presiaed in the Crown Court, congratulated the grand jury on the fact that there was an exceptionally light calendar. In the course of the day his Lordship sentenc.,cl a man named Johnson to 18 months' imprisonment for unlawfully wound- ing a little boy, his nephew. Whilst suffering from delirium tremens, the prisoner cut the boy's throat with a knife, and then attempted to commit suicide. An Oldham Operative named Marron who, without any provocation, had kicked a boy upon the head with his clog, was committed for eight months. A shocking case of neglect on the part of a mother occupied the attsntion of the court. The woman was addicted to drink, and had allowed the child, which was only seven weeks old, to starve. It was said that when told the child was in fits, the mother said, "It doesn't matter; it's in a club ;" but no evidence was offered to show that the child was in a club or that she had received any money on account of its death. She was sentenced to 12 months' im- prisonment. A post-office official was sentenced to penal servitude for five years for stealing a letter containing MO. Mr. Justice Lopes presided In the Nisi Prins Court. The cause list Is unusually light. FORTY MORE DEATHS FROM SUNSTROKE. A telegram from Cincinnati, on Wednesday, says :—The heat is intense here and in other western cities. Business is at a standstill. Ninety-nine cases of sunstroke occurred yes- terday, and 40 deaths. CINCINNATI, JULY 13.-1 hirty-five deaths occurred here to-day from excessive beat. The present mortality has been equalled only by the rate during occasional epidemics.
The business of the Manekester Summer Assizes

CHESHIRE CROP Preosracrs. Lovely harvest wenther set in on Monday, and hay cutting is now general through- out the county: Everywhere the crop is retorted light, the sweet bottoin grass being very short and thin. Clover, on the contrary, is uniformly excellent, and will very fairly compensate farmers for an unusually light hay-grass crop. In consequence of a very late swing, cheese-making goal_ rnenced late;, and Mr. Joseph Aston, of Brassey Green, who lives in the centre of a clieese country, reports that the turn- out this year will be one-fourth below the average. Depres- ! Sian has had something to do with this, many farmers having been compelled to mince their herds in order to find money for rent. The maogold plant is seriously affected ; with the maggot, many fields looking as if the plant had ! been cut down by frost. In heavy clay soils it is doubtful 1 if they will recover the check they have received. In many instances turnips have been sown twice and thrice over, the , young plants having been eaten up by the fly as soon as they ;Ippesred. Potatoes, of which immen: quantities are , grown, ,in Cheshire for the Liverpool and , Manchester ; markets, are found to be fairly cropping, and at present to be unaffected by disease.

Witness: lam speaking with " fairation"; but it is very I bard for a man to speak every word— , Superintendent of Police: That is all rubbish; just answer the question. • , Witness: I cannot say. The Coroner (to witness): Now you must know. Just attend to what I sap. What you said just now was that you never saw her badly drunk, but that you had seen her in drink.
Witness: Yes. The Coroner: How often in the week? Witness (in a ruminating manner) : Oh, how 'often in the week ?

The Corcner: Now, come, there arq only seven days in a week. unless you can manage to make eight out of them. Witness! Some weeks. she would appear a little "unsensible." It might be with drink, but I 4annot say!' I , could not tell what it was with. The Coroner: Was it -with abuse, do you think?

.froe of the most curious reasons for disinclination to prosecute for felony that I have ever heard was brought to my notice the other day. A man broke the window of a grocer's shop, and ran away with a jar of jam. A gentler- man who was passing at the time chased the thief for a con- siderable distance, and, haying succeeded in capturing his man, brought him back, when the woman who owns the shop said she should not prosecute the fellow, for she "bad children of her own who might get into trouble some day." It is fortunate that every one is not quite so considerate of the future of his children as this grocer.

I am pleased to learn that the registration in connection with the whole of South-West Lancashire is now being thoroughly looked after4n the Liberal interest. The Liberal party' organisation has been completely revised, and in ad- dition to having good registration agents in each district, they have now an excellent and energetic and experienced Liberal worker as secretary in the person of Mr. G. H. Powell, who has teen well educated in the Birmingham school.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. THE IRISH LAND BILL.—Mr. GLAnwroans, in reply to a question, said at present it was not intended to declare urgency as regarded the passage of the Irisb Land Bill. THE TuArrsvAta..—Mr. sarAngrows said it would not be possible to take the debate on the Transvaal on Monday. He would devote Thursday to it. The committee on the Land Bill would be closed, as he hoped, on Wednesday.— Sir H. BEACH said be would consider whether, under the circumstances, it would not be desirable to postpone the dabate until a later period. Vourwrinita Rzynew IN SCOTLAND.-Mr. CHILDERS said the Queen would review volunteers in the Queen's Park, Edinburgh, on the 25th August. - -

MR. LABOI7CHERE AND THE SPEAKER.—Mr. LsnorcnKnit asked why a question of his did not appear on the paper.— The SPEAKER said because it contained an attack on the Prince of Bulgaria.—Mr. LABOUCHERE rose and said he would conclude with a motion.—The SPEAKER said if under cover of a motion he intended to reopen the question, he would not put his motion from the chair.—bfr. Lnor- CHERE said i.e would refer to the subject next session. THE LAND BILL—The House then went into Committee en the Irish Land Bill.—Clause 21: Supply of money for the land commission was postponed.—Clauses 28 to 30 agreed to without amendment.—Clause 31, which com- menced part six of the bill, which dealt with court and land commission, was proposed. The clause dealt with the description of the court and its proceedings.—Mr. BIGGAR moved an amendmet to associate two persons elected by Parliamentary votes to assist the court when holding sittings [LEFT SITTING.]

HEALTH or WABEINGTON.—The health of Warring- ton for the week ending the 9th lust, has been such that the death rate was the lowest that has ever been known, viz., 6.3 per thousand. This is actually lower than the death- rate in Dr. Richardson's ideal city, in which he says the death-rate should not exceed 8 per thousand. • BAPTIST CHAPEL, LATCHIPORD.—In connection with this place of worship sermons were preached on Sunday, morning and evening, by the Rev. John Howe, of Water- barn. There were largesongregations at each service, and the collections in aid of the school and church funds realized about £22. On Tuesday the Sunday scholars had their annual trip. The teachers and scholars, numbering about 140, accompanied by a few friends, started from Bank Quay Station about 11 o'clock for Acton Bridge, the pat tv imme- diately on arrival proceeding to the farm of Mr. Hough, where dinner wasprovided for the children. Being favoured with fine weather, a pleasant afternoon was spent in 'w' Ina which d had aadn di increased ds to eaenbo:u* t A2booou, t rfi:: ea so'secml obcike dthefoprartteav,. preparations afterwards being made for home, which was reached ehortly after eight o'clock. the outing having been thoroughly enjoyed. WARRIMITON PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY Scoots.—The scholars attending the above schools were favoured with glorious summer weather for their asnual trip. which took place on Monday last, to Blackpool. The train left Bank Quay s'atifin about seven a.m.,,and the excursionists, of whom there were not so many as in previous years, were accompanied by the Rector and Mrs. Quekett, the Rev F. W. Cory, superintendent of the girls' school, and the 11'2V. J. H. Davies, superintendent of the boys' school After a splendid ride of about two hours. the .trippere arrived at their destination, and dispersed to find amusement at the varied attractions provided at this popular health resort. The teachers, churchwardens, Messrs. Dooley and Davies, secretary, Mr. Scotson, and several other friends lunched together in the schoolroom adjoining Christ Church, which ths vicar, the Rev. Mr. Wainwright, also placed at the dis- posal of the rector and teachers is the aftet noon for tea. A most enjoyable day was spent, and the homeward journey was commenced in the evening about 7-30, and concluded about ten o'clock, when the party arrived in Warringtor. well satisfied with their excursion.

The MASTER reported that there were 495 inmates, as against 455 in the corresponding week of last year. During the week 190 vagrants-139 men, 31 women, and 20 chil- dren—had been relieved. The Master called the attention of the Guardians to the irregular mode of putting forward accounts for payment for goods supplied to the barracks, some of which passed throuh his books, but others be neither saw the goods nor bills: This, he felt, placed him in a false position in having: to explain at the auditing of his :accounts ma'to-rs over which he had no control, besides being very unpleasant and annoying to both the Guardians and himself. The CHAIRMAN remarked that the difficulty would bo removed by the resolution of the Board. THE SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICER. Mr. WotsrANLEi said be happened to be one of the depu- tation from this Board winch went to Broadmoor to examine tasylum t the lunatics they had there. They found that out of the four lunatics 'the Boahradhbaedent heel-0e; townottwe de quiterteo he inoffensive. for stealing a young mail, ,mat boots. nh When he was arraigned at Liver- pool he was acquitted on the ground of insanity, and he had been in the asyium nine yearS, and the Board bad been pay- ing 14s. a sieek towards his support —[Mr. MaCICIE : Shame !]—and it cost the country 6s. a week extra. Througn the exertions they made they got two of the persons removed to Prestwich. He had no doubt whatever that if the Board would rake action they would be able to get one of the boys sent to this house. He wonld maintain himself inste,d of the Board having to maintain him. While at the asylum he asked the governor "How is it that while they can at our county asylutics maintain lunatics at a cost of something like 9s or 108 a week, you charge nearly 30s ?" The answer was, "You see here, we are obliged to keep so many attendants. Instead of having one to 13 inmates, which is the average at our county asylums, we have one to five. Criminal lunaticsare always anxious to make their escape." He said, "I have been to many lunatic asylums, but I never met with a luna- tic who did not want to escape." Another reason for the expensive charge was, he said, because the establishment was under the care of two masters. The fabric was under the care of the Bard of Woks, but the inmates were under the supervision of the Home Secretary. One authority could not interfere with the other, and instead of making use of luna,ic labour tradespeople had to be employed. The Board made a strong remonstrance to Sir R. A. Cross, and he was glad to say the Board of Works gave way, and they now allowed p mper labour to be made use of. The doctor told the depttratyn the result up to the time they vis:ted -.ved. He believed if an

them was that MOO had been save... easquiry were made the cost of maintenance would be materi- ally reduced. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE thought the Board ought to take every step they could to get their criminal pauper patients re- moved from Broadmoor, and the Board would be clear ef them. Mr. COOPER reminded the Board that one pauper was at Broaimoor for child murder, and no removal could take After a few further renlarks from Mr. Winstanley, the I subject dropped. • THE MT= GE CHECKING ACCOUNTS. Mr. Woomate. called the attention of the Board to the fact that a great many of the accounts had not been duly certified. The Clearnuate : Not certified by anyone? 1111 r. WOOLFALL said they were not certified by Mr. Mackey. There was just a lump sum on some of the bills, which did not show whether it was for the barracks or not. Major CARTWRIGHT said the system had begun again after what had transpired between the auditor and what had transpired between the two establishments. The same thing he believed occurred last week that ac- counts were being paid now, that had never been certified at all. The Board would recollect the case they had a short time ago in regard to some hats from some one in Wigan. The very same thing occurred there—he meant they were certified in such a way that the bill—which was a perfectly legal bill but had not boen properly entered—wag notified by the auditor, and caused much unpleasantness with a mem- ber of the Board who absolutely charged him with being mean. [Mr. Winstanley Hear, hear.] No doubt Mr.Win- stanley would say "hear." What was the meaning of his being charged with meanness? Simply this, that he had said or hinted that there was some collusion between the• party 19140 said "hear, hear" (Mr. Winstanley) and the Clerk as to the payment of that account. Well, he asked every member of the Board whether he made any allusion of that sort, at all. What difference did it make to him or any member of the Board, if a person sent in a bill and was paid the next week? It was not fair to keep peeple who dealt with the Board out of their ac- Counts, and he should propose that, instead of accounts be- ing paid zig zag as at present, they should be paid at the first meeting of ;he Board after the expiration of one month. He was praceeding to state that he was sorry to say some people received accounts when they had not done their work in a proper manner, when Mr. WINSTANLEY Said: It's a lie. The CHAIRMsN: I call upon you to retiact that observa- tion. Mr. WINSTANLEY did retract it and /aid his temper got the better of him. But the statement was not true. Mr. GARNETT remarked that a good deal had been said that ought not to have been said. In reference to the question Mr. Woolfall rose to speak upon, it was a very important question, and one that could not be overstated. As Major Cartwright said, men had no right to be kept waiting for their money. [Major Cartwright: Certainly not.] But there had been to say the least of it, a little inattention that some of the accounts had not been thoroughly audited and certified. He thought there was perhaps a little blame attaching to the Clerk who shoold not be ready to put his blue peuell upon any account until Mr. Mackey had certified it as being correct. Until that was done hc would not nalea single ReCOnnt. Maier CARTWRIGHT said he Was perhaps a little Out of order in referring to a matter which he intended to speak about when tbe minutes of the House Committee came be- fore them, but he was not so mean as to immediately corn_ plain of the work, hut had given every opportunity for the work to be properly finished, but they absolutely refused to do so, although the architect had condemned the work. Still, the abusive Mileage Mr. Winstanley had thought prcper to make use of Ind now he took for what it was. worth. The CHAIRMAN : Mr. Winstanley withdrew the observa- tion. Major CARTWRIGHT: Did he? I did not bear him. The CHAIRMAN: Yes, I nailed upon him and he did, with that good :sense which generally distinguishes his delibera- tions, at once withdraw it. Mr. GARNETT : Don't let us have it gone into further. Mr. WINSTANLEY: I think I have a right to make a remark in reference to that bill, which has been referred to several times. It happened to be a bill of my daugh- ter's Mr. GARNETT: A fortnight ago you made the same explanation. The Dceerry CLERK said the whole of the accounts that bad been objected to by Mr. Woolfall were accounts either for goods supplied to the house or the barracks. They had been entered in the master's day book, and be bad received them from Ms bands, but if the master bad not certified thein he could not help it. The CIIAIRUAN : But when you find an account has not been certified by the master, is it not rather premature to .pay it? Mi. GLIINETT : That is the point. A desultory discussion in reference to the checking of the Accounts then took place, and several times the whole of the members appeared to be talking at once. Mr. GREENING said the system seemed to him to be a complete maddle. If the Board paid their accounts monthly as other people did, it would be a much better system. The MASTER said he signed for all goods he received at the workhouse, but he objected to be a kind of machine for registering things he knew nothing about. Mr. GARNETT said the accounts for the barracks and the workhouse should be kept separate—(hear, hear)—and the accounts for the barracks signed by Mr. Mines. Mr. DARBYSHIRE said the question had been settled by the Local Government Board contrary to Mr. Garnett's suggestion. It was ultimately moved by the Rev. J. YONGE that the clerk be instructed to submit the matter to the Local Govern- ment Board for their decision. Mr. WooLFALL seconded the motion, which was carried. THE POWER TO REDUCE SALARIES. A letter was read from the Sleaford Union asking the Board to appoint a gentleman to co-operate with. represen- tatives to be appointed by other Boards of Guardians to bring the que,tion of power to reduce the salaries of.nniop officers before the Local Government Board. Mr. WINSTANLEY proposed that the letter lie on the table, and Mr. GREENING seconded the proposition. Mr. DARBYSIIIIIE proposed an amendment that the Board I take action on the matter when the time arrived. Meacert CARTWRIGHT seconded the amendment vhich. after some conversation, was passed, the Clerk being instructed to reply that the object met with the ap:mmval of the Board. STRANGE CONDUCT OF AN ASYLUM OFFICIAL. Mr. WI/imam:Ey said that last week the Newton relieving' officer told the committee that the clerk to the Ilaydock ' Lodge Asylum had been over to him and told him there was a lunatic in the asylum whose husband had not paid any- thing for her support for a considerahle time and he was going to hand her over to Mr. Caldwell. Mr. Caldwell very properly told him he had nothing to do with the case, and he should refuse to have anything to do with it. The officio staid he would bring her down to the office on Saturday and.

WARRINGTON POLICE CASES. BATURDAT.—Before Alderman Burgess and Alderman Chandley, THE BEGGING NUISANCE—TWO ragged little urchins named Thomas Garritty and John Birmingham, were charged with begging in Wilson-Patten-street, and Parker- street, on the Bth inst.—P. C. Pace deposed to seeing the prisoners go to the front and back doors of several houses in' the streets named, and beg.—The mothers of the prisoners appeared, and Mr.„Hunt, who asked where the fathers were, said he locked the little fellows up for the purpose of getting 1 at the parents, so that the magistrates could commit them, instead of these little children.— Alderman Chandley: Quite right, too.—Mr. Hunt said the prisoners acted in a very adroit manner, and that showed something more than begging. The parents were more to blame' than the lads, and he was determined if possible to get at the parents.— Alderman Burgess remarked that Mr. Hunt was quite right in so doing, as the neighbourhood was infested with old women and children.—Mr. Hunt said the parents of one of the children had been summoned for neglecting to send his children to school.—Alderman Burgess: They are in train- ing for this work, undoubtedly.—ln reply to the Bench, Garritty said he went to beg at the invitation of Birming- ham, and the latter said he went on his own account and took home what money he got to buy bread with.—Alder- man Burgess said it was very deplorable to see the children in their present condition, which showed there was not the slightest care taken of them.—The prisoners were remanded Until Monday. AN OFFENSIVE " VaLENTlNE."—Winifred Maloney, a young woman, was charged en warrant with having, on the • Bth inst., assaulted Mary Clark.—The parties are fustian cutters, and the defendant, according to complainant, on Thursday, "took a knife and hit her across the head twice," breaking the knife with the blows. Complainant took out . . .

a summons against defendant, and on Friday morning, de- fendant went to her and said, "You have sent me a valentine, have not you," and as she was going up the stairs to the shop, defendant "collared her," and hit her on the eye, which she greatly discoloured.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months, herself in .£5 and one surety in a like amount, or in default, 14 days' imprison- ment. ALLEGED SYSTEMATIC HOTEL ROBBERY.— Annie Foy and Elizabeth Seddon, married women, were charged with steal- ing from the Patten Arms Hotel, on or about the let ult., a quantity of upholsterer's lace, figured-damask, repp-damask, oil stair-cloth, 3 knives, 3 forks, 6 spoons, Ste., value about 155., the property of Miss Annie Wooliscroft,the manageress; and Thomas Foy. husband of the first named prisoner, was charged with stealing from the premises of Messrs. iobert Collin and Sons, Academy-street, 3 scaffold ropes, value 31., and•further with stealing, or receiving, knowing them to be stolen, the property his wife was charged with stealing.— ,Mr. Hunt called evidence to justify a remand, and the Bench remanded the- prisoners until Tuesday, but admitted to bail Mrs. Seddon, she having recently been confined. MONDAY.—Before Aldermen Holmes and Burgess and Councillor Fairclough. CAUGHT IN A TRAP.—Henry Hankinson was charged with stealing a quantity of oilcloth, value 183., the property of James Moore.—From the statement of the Chief Con- stable, it appeared that the prosecutor was an oil-cloth dealer, living at St. Helens, and attended the Warrington market on Wednesdays. On the 25th May the prisoner was seen about the market aeveral times during the day, and the prosecutor thinking he was a steady young man entrusted him with a roll of oil-cloth, value 183., to take to Mr.Toft's, in Horsemarket-street. The prisoner, however, did not return With the 18s., and he was not seen until Saturday, when be was apprehended by P.S. Cox. Prisoner tried to escape by flirting up an entry, but, as there was only one • ' '

ment Boat . ~acane by running up no. -- June, 1882, of Mr. Benjamin Hobson, as sch'ool attendance means of ingrees and egress ha was" walled in." (Laughter., g Officer of the Warrington Union, at a salary of £75 per. R. Toft deposed to givin the prisoner 18s., fo annum. which he did not ere her a Teeeipt,—The prisoner was com- mitted for three months' hard labour. DOING "A HANDY TFIING."—TIMMaS Farrington was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket- street, with refusing to quit the Ram's Head, Horsemarket- street, and with assaulting P.C. Monaghan.—About 20 minutes past eight on Saturday night P.C. Monaghan was called into the Ram's Head to quell a disturbance. He was putting the,men out when the prisoner caught hold of him and said, "You are not going to do that," and struck him. Prisoner, who was drunk, refused to leave when requested, and the assistance of four or five policemen was required to convey him to the police station.—The person who repre- sented the landlady said he sent for the policeman, and he was sure the prisoner had no drink whilst in the house ;—at least, he believed not, as he did not serve hitn.--The Chief Constable: A man sits down in a public-house for an hour or two, and when he becomes refractory a policeman is sent for to put him out. That is a handy thing to do, and tells two ways. There are Many complaints about this sort of of thing at the Ram's Head. We had a similar case to this before the magistrates a few days ago.—Alderman Burgess: It is not known to the police what condition the man was in when he went to the house ?—The Chief Constable : No, sir.—The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk, 10s. and costs for refusing to quit, and 20s. and costs for the assault on the police, or in default two months' imprison- ment stitk hard labour. . A RUNAWAY HUSBAND—Michael Mayer WAS brought up on warrant charged with having, on the 28th March, run away and left his wife and family chargeable to the com- mon fund of the Warrington Union.—The prisoner said he went to Stockport in search of work, and when he returned. he found that " his old woman " had go'ne to the Work- house.—Mr. Harbourne, relieving officer, said the amount owing to the Union was £(3 153. 4d. The defendant was earning 12e. a week.—The case was adjourned for a month, to enable the defendant to make arrangements with Mr. Har- bourne to take his wife out of the 'house. OBTAINING MONEY BY FALSE PRETENCES. Martha Clare was charged with obtaining ss. by false pretences.— Mary Ann iLane, the prosecutnx, is the recipient of relief , from the Union, and on Saturday morning she sent a woman named Hardman to the relieving officer foi the money. When she was returning the prisoner met her and said she , would take charge of the mciney, which WAS given to her, ' but which had not been handed over to Mrs. Lane.—The prisoner, who said she did not intend to retain the money, was ordered to return it, the magistrates stating that a con- viction would be recorded against her. UNREGISTERED LODGING-ROUSES: A DISGRACEFUL CASE. An old man, named Patrick Island, residing in Silver-square, was charged with keepina lodgers in his house, which was un- registered. Inspector Church said the house was not registered, and one more person slept in it than it could be registered for. The case was adjourned fer a month.— William Loden, of Wainwright's-yard, was charged with a similar offence. Mr. Ralph Norman, sanitary Inspector, sail when he visited the house, he found in one bed the de- fendant and his wife. In another bed were two men—one I the defendant's son and the other a lodger—and at the foot lay two women, both sexes being almost in a state of nudity. There was no ventilation in the room, and the house was in a filthy condition.—Defendant Was fined 20s. and costs. For like offences, Catherine Burke was fined 20s. and costs, Patrick Saxon 10s. and costs, and Mary Power ss. and COAL Wire Ass/vim—Thomas Murphy was charged with as. esaultitig and beating his wife, Mary Murphy. P.C. Crickett said be saw the defendant in Horsernarket-street on Saturday evening. His wife was nying to persuade him to go home when he turned round and struck her in a savage manner. His wife, however, had refused to appear against him.—The Ex-Mayor: Was he drunk at the time? Wit- ness: He had been drinking—The defendant said he pushed his wife, but he did not strike her.—He was bound over to keep the peace. AN EXPENSIVE NIGHT's LODGING.—Thomas Sinister was charged being drunk at the police station: The prisoner went into the police station on Saturday night, and asked for I xlgings. He was told that was not a lodging house, but he then said" Well, if you won't give me a night's lodging, I will be locked up." The police,therefore, complied with his wish and locked him up.—For his lodging the Bench ordered him to pay ss. . A PRIsONER WITH A PECULIARITY.—JeIin Cartledge WAS charged with bi ing drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket- street.—The Chief Constable said this was the prisoner's thirtieth appearance before the court.—Alderman Holmes: This is the fourth time you have been here this year.—The Chief Constable said there was one peculiarity about the prisoner which gave a great deal of trouble to the police, tend it "as that he never answered his summonses, and a , warrant had always to be issued for his apprehension. On this occasion, he failed to answer to the summons as usual, but he had surrendered to the warrant. —Councillor Fair- dough (to the prisoner): You put the police to a great deal of trouble.—Prisone:: But I gave myself up this time.— The Chief Constable: Not at tirst.—Tbe prisoner was fined 20s. and costs, with the option of a month's imprisonment. AN IDLE VAGRANT SENT TO Gam Ann Broughton was charged, being an inmate of the casual ward of the War- rington Union, with refnsing to perform the task set her by the workhouse master. The defendant, when called by the portress in the usual way on Monday morning, refused to get up. When at last she did get up a task of the usual kind was set her, but she refused to do it, and used very bad language to the portrese, whom she called very opprobrious names.—The prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days. TUESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley, and Major Cartwright. THE ROBBERY FROM THE PATTEN ARMS HOTEL—Annie Foy, and Elizabeth Seddon were charged on remand with stealing from the Patten Arms Hotel, on the Ist ult., a quantity of upholsterer's lace, damask, dm., the property of Miss Wooliscroft; Annie Foy was further charged with stealing from the same hotel, about the 15th April, a black coat and vest, value 305., and two table covers, value 3a., the property of Miss Wooliscroft and another, and Thomas Foy WAS charged with stealing from the premises of Messrs Robert Collin and Sons, Academy-street, three scaffold ropes, value 35., and further with stealing or receiving the property stolen by his wife.—On Monday, the 4th inst., a woman named Elizabeth Marsh, reported to the police the loss or robbery of a dress, value 308. front her house in Ellesmere-street; alrlninsg wHPheiocarhltseord-isfdtoruennt;l.l where the prisoners lived. Mrs. Foy had been in the habit of visiting Mrs. Marsh, but at this time she left town for Chester. On her return Inspector Singleton called upon three ropes, a bridle, head gear, &c., in the house, and as he iastnedntobwsietzetdheiinr pthoesithinonusein gloiored reported the loss of seemrMi mr Mrs. Foy, mFe b e„,o such articles, the male prisoner, who was employed by that firm as a carter, was locked up. The inspector afterwards consistent Messrs. Collin and Son had went to Mrs. Seddon's house, and found there goods similar to those discovered at Mrs. Foy's house, and the result was that the prisoners were locksd up on a charge of stealing the property. The female prisoners had been employed by Miss Wooliscroft, the talwageresa of the hotel, and this lady on

LETTER FROM TUE TAILOR. A letter was read from Mr. S. Greenway, stating that be bad beard the Board was wanting a tailor in his place at the workhouse, and he begged to be allowed to go there to his old shop and the work he had been used to for over 16 .years. If they would kindly consider his application, and the circumstances he was placed in, having a sick wife who would be unable to go to Padgate, he felt 'ci...rtain this Board would allow him what he asked for, as he felt sure none of the Guardians would like to see him thrown out of a situa- tion when the children left the barracks for Padgate. A short conversation ensued, and the It v: John Yonge was directed to intimate to Mr. Greenw,, that whatever assistance was required at the house ,woud be of a tem- porary character, and if he was in the same circumstances when an aprointment was made the Board would consider
liis application. •

- - REV. E. C. E. CARLETE ON SCHOOL BOARDS.—MR. MIINDELLA'S "CAVALIER" TREATMSST. Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON reported the interview that took plane between the deputation and Mr. Mundella. on Monday, respecting the payment of school fees of poor children. He did not think Mr. Mundella treated with much ceremony the gentlemen who appeared before him, though there was no doubt there would be great practical difficulty in his way, as Parliament was hampered with busi- ness. What be objected to waa the evident desire and in- tention of Mr. Mundell:l—and it had been done more than once—to fotce School Boards upon districts where they did not at present exist. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Mundella seemed to give the impression—in fact he intimated such in so many words—that ths establi•htnent of School Boards would be a way out of the difficulty, and in concluding said he would be more in sympathy with the members of the depu- tation if they came forward with a declaration in favour of universal School Boards. He did not think they would he prepared to adopt School Boards out of cbmpliment to Mr. Mundella. The first consideration was the welfare of the district, but Mr. Mundella seemed to be unaware of the fact that School Boards were not very popular, that they were not on the increase, but in places where they had been tried they had been given up. and only a few weeks ago they had reported the case of Tamworth School Board where the Bbard were in great difficulty and had not money to pay' their officials. He thought under the circumstances they ought not to be compelled to adopt School Boards simply out of compliment to Mr. Mundella. Rev. J. YONOE : I rise to a point of order. May I ask. is Xr_. Carleton "ving to conclude with a motion? Bev. E. C. E. CARLETON ; Yes. Rev. J. Yoscan said it was an importaht subject, and one they would all like to discuss, but as he had not had an op- portunity of reading the discussion he asked would it not be better to give notice of motion and discuss the matter at

the next meeting. Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON then gave notice of motion, but as it was ruled that he could address the Board in giving notice he proceeded to remark that he thought there was no necessity for a School Board in Warrington because hitherto they had had gentlemen of public spirit and benevolence who had been willing to spend their means for the purpose of furthering education without burdening the taxpayers— gentlemen like Mr. Beamont, and Mr. John Crosfield who had very generously • come forward in the case of the Peo- ple's College. He thought the present system ef legisla- .tion tended to dry up theee private sources of liberality, and the fact was there would be no channel in which they could expend their money except in political agitation. He pro- tested against this system because he thought it would rob the poor of that charity which they would under ordinary circumstances be allowed to enjoy. It was against the whole 1 system he objected. It was not as if School Boards had been more succeesfnl than volantary schools, because that was not the case even on the testimony of Mr. Mundella, who showed in a speech Ist made last year, the results of the grant obtained per heso. in Board schools as compared svith volue,tary schools. In Board schools they obtained 10s.i. 31<1., and in voluntary schools 15s. &id., and to put against the farthing was the religious instruction that was given. Voluntary schools, without costing the people any- thing like that amount, were doing (rite as good a work as , IBtpasioapebacnayre. ildst iyisl ilecel (whose owl sods ueanol , cinr not ti:et Igsv ithtnteesocinnae:v rep attempt twid e, xti nelopen, 1 rrc. efeeos sr cesoiei if r b. there Ms: :raiwh. unoano:odll ruenginaoi Boards necessity 18aellraldtoisno gn edu,,p,himself. efto rooner , such that were now, he believed, pretty well rejected), who • believed School Boards ought to be compulsory all over the • country whether the people like it or not. To make that I doctrine go dowu they maintained the outlay world simply ; be id. in the t: History had completely falsified that doc- trine and the result was School Boards were not very popular. He did not know why Mr. Mundella should treat them so cavalierly, and say they could not do anything unless they came to his view. The motion of which he gave notice was that "Seeing little may be expected from Parliament it is the opinion of the Board that the Town Council should endeavour to give effect to the views put before Mr. Mundella by that deputation without going, if possible, to Parliament, even if they have to strain the law a little." Rev. J. YONGE supposed Mr. Carlton would put the motion in a rather better strain than that. He did not like the last sentence, and confessed he would not like a motion submitted to the Board which went in favour of straining the law. Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON would simply say that the War- rington Guardians and Town Council do the best they can to get out of the difficulty. THE EXPOUNDED CHARGE AGAINST THE PORTER. Major CARTWRIGHT drew attention to the charge which had been preferred against the porter in which he had to em- ploy a solicitor at the cost of tl Is., and he suggested that Mr. Curry should be recouped that outlay. The CHAIRMAN explained that an unprincipled, bad woman had simply persecuted the porter, and proposed that the II is. be paid out of the " Nemo" fund. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE seconded the proposition, which was carried.

THE ALTERATIONS AT THE HOUSE.—SERIOUS ALLEGATIONS. Major CARTWRIGHT. in moving the adoption of the minutes of the House Committee, referred to a contract that had been entered into with a Mr.Winstanley, of Newton, for alterations at the hospital, and he alleged that the work had been unsatisfactorily done. He also stated that the whol.• of the money due to the contractor had been paid with the exception of about £3. A discussion took place on the matter, and Mr. GREEN - IN, I proposed that the Clerk be instructed to write to Mr Owen, the architect, asking him to report on the quality of the work, and the amount of money paid. Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON seconded the motion, which was carried.

The DEPUTY CLEns. said Mr. Owen desired him to inform the Board that he had wrii ten to the contractor arid told him that the work was 11,4 in a satisfactory condition, and mikes he put it right he would have it done and charge him vith the cost.

being called as a witness identified the hpholstery. damask, table cloths, spoons, Wc., as property belonging to the hotel, but said she never authorised either of the female prisoners to remove any of the goods—in fact she had cautioned them not to do so.—Wm. Thomas Lickfold, barman at the hotel tap, identified the coat and vest, mentioned in the charge, as his imperty.—A second search was made in the prisoners' houses on Monday, and at Foy's P.C. Neill found eight pawn tickets relating to goods pledged at Mmes. Greaves', Ver- non's arid Jackson's pawnshops.—Mr. Cranway, in the employ of Messrs. Collin arta Son, said he ksued ropes to ithe workmen, and theta was nothing e‘traardinary in the carter having them in his house.--The Bench decided to deal with the case summarily.—Mr. G. T. Moore, who ap- peared for the prisoners, then addressed the Bench on their behalf. He called Martin Foy, who said the bridle, bead gear, and horse rug produced were his property. and he left them at his brother's house.—Alderman Chandley said the Bench had no hesitation in coming the conclusion that the female prisoners were guilty, and they were each sen- tenced to two months' imprisonment with hard labour. As to the male prisoners, all the circumstances were extremely suspicious, but as they had not been able to prove anything against him he would be disaharged.—The hearing of the case occupied over two hours, and the court was well filled with spectators.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Captain Litton and Councillor Fairclough. _

THE BEGGING NIIISANCE.—Johu rawley, a young lad, was charged with be4ging in Bold-street, at four o'clock on the previous day.—The boy was remanded to the work- house for a fortnight to ascertain if he could be put under the proper control of his parents.—For a similar offence, Elizabeth Harrison was sent to prison for 14 days. THEFT FROM A LODGING HOUSE—John Dolan, a farm labourer, was charged with stealing from Michael•McHugh, lodging house keeper, Hill-street, two bed quilts and asheet, of the value of ss. Prisoner bad been lodging with prose- cutor for about three weeks, and on Monday he took the articles named from off the bed on which he had been sleep-

_ tore them into shreds, and sold them as rags to dr. Mulhall, marine store dealer, Winwick-street.—The Bench commented strongly upon the action of Mulhall in not call- ing in police when he received such suspicious articles.— Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month with hard labour.

ASSAULT UPON A COUNTY CO.URT BAILIFF—Mary Ann Dollard, a widow, was charged, under a warrant, with assaulting Thos. McQuinn, a county court bailiff —Mr. Moore, jun., appeared for• the prosecutor.—On Mon- day last, shortly after one o'clock, prosecutor and another bailiff went to prisoner's house to serve an execution upon her goods. She was very drunk, and stating the house was not hers, tried to push the prosecutor out of the house. He then despatched his assistant for a policeman, and in the meantime prisoner took a tin can from the mantel piece, and struck prosecutor on the face, and abused him "shamefully." rn the struggle McQninn's watch was taken, and had not been recovered.—Benjimin Blinston, high bailiff, said that when he got back to the house with the officer there were about a hundred women struggling to get the prosecutor away from the woman, and on him going near they pulled him down.—Captain Litton said it appeared two strong men like the bailiffs could have kept the women quiet.—Mr. Moore said they were not allowed —Mr. Hunt remarked that if it had been anyone else they would not , have gone to that house without a policeman.—Captain Litton: They could have sent for one.—Mr. Hunt said the women congregated in crowds in a very short time, and nothing, caused more bother than a lot of women knocking about. (Laughter.) When the prosecutor went to the police office be appeared to have been much abused and palled about, and blood was flowing from cuts on his fee.— The Bench did not think the bailiffs had excerded their duty, and as the woman had not been up before they would deal lenitktly with her, and fine her 10s. and costs, or in de- fault 11 days.

THE MID-CHESHIRE SALT AND CHEMICAL COMPANY, LIMITED. In our last, issue we referred to the incorporation of the above Company, under the Coutpanies' Acts, with a capital of £250,000 in shares of £5 each, for the purpose of erecting works on an eligible site of freehold land on which brine springs exist (adjacent to both canal and railway) at Kin- derton, Middlewich, in the county of Chester, and there carrying on the business of salt and chemical manufacturers on a very extensive scale. Almost every one is aware that great deposits of rock-salt exist in the county of Chester, and the solution of this rock-salt forms brine which is raised or pumped from the deposits and manufactured by evapora- tion into salt for home and foreign consumption. t We glean, however, from the North of England Mining Journal that this Company intends to adopt the best .machinery methods and patents which may be invented from time to time for the manufacture of both salt and chemicils, and a scheme for the manufacture of salt by deposition or precipitation without the aid of fuel, has already been offered to the dite3tot s. We also understand the patent has been secured, and that no expensive iron or steel pans, as at p-esent used, will be nscsssary for the new process of manufacture but that the salt from the brine raised from the Company's land can be made at a nominal coit by deposition or precipitation in pans or vessels built or made in an inexpensive manner from wood or earthenware. If this scheme is feasable it may, as stated by the North of Eng!and Mining Journal lead to a complete revolution in the present process of salt manufacture, and will nedoubt at the same time tend to rid the district of the present snroke nuisance. The Cheshire salt district may be said to have practically the monopolvof ' supplying the world with 'Salt, furnishing as it does 1,000,000 tons per annum for export from Liverpool, and upwards of 400,000 tons to the chemical works of Widnes and other towns. We are informed that there were exported 539,044 tons of white salcfrom the ports of the Mersey in the six months ending the 30th June last, and that during the past month there were exported from Weston Point and Runcorn (shipping ports at the mouth of the Weaver from the Ches'tire salt district) 40,757 tons of white salt, which is the largest shipment ever made in one month from these ports. To the lame and to Widnes where there are large chemical works requiring vast quantities ef salt, or where it is the principal factor in the articles manufactured, the cost' of carriage adds considerably' to the cost of production. It will therefore be seen that as this company intend to manu- facture chemicals at Middlewich as well as salt, a great sav- ing in carriage alone will be effected, and it is said that the new undertaking cannot fail to be successful. With such a vasttimount of raw material for several chemical products at band, the company Will be able to entet with vigonr and enterprise into the manufacture. At this present time we import, more especially from Germany, a vast amount of chemicals if which salt forms the basis, and there is no reason, .that with abundance of salt at hand why these should not be produced at home, and we wish the" Mid- Cheshire Salt and Chemical Company Limited ". every suc- cess. The directorate is a strong and influential one. Parr's Banking Company Limited and its branches are the hankers to the company, and we are of opinion the anticipations of the directors that the capital of the company will earn a minimum profit of 15 per ceut, per annum will be fully realized. The first issue of capital for public subscription is 15,000 seven and a half per cent. nreference shares of £5 each. This preference dividend of 7:4, per cent, per annum forms the first change on the profits available for dividends, and these preference shams (after a similar dividend has been paid on the ordinary shares), are entitled to further participation in profits. The attention of our readers and of investors is directed to the prospectus of the company from which it will he seen, that the directors are of opinion that the shires will be a sound anti lucrative investment.

LYM3I LOCAL BOARD.—A. special meeting of this Board was held on Thursday under the presidency of Mr. Cameron, to receive and discuss further plans and suggsstions as to the sewerage scheme. There were present Messrs. Rogers, Simpson, Hall, Richardson, Gibbon, and Appleton. Messrs. Brockbank, Wilson, and Mulliner had, however, forwarded neither plans nor report, and it was decided to hold another special meeting on Thursday next.—A. number of tenders had been received for the supplying of coal for the gas works. The tender of Messrs. Fletcher, Burrows and Co. for 403 tons was accepted on the motion of Mr. Rogers, seconded by Mr. Richardson.

INQUEST AT LVM.M.—At the Millstone Inn. Lymm, on Saturday last, an inquest Was held .before Mr. T. J. Ridg- way, coroner, on the body of Thomas Houghton, 71 years of age, whose body was found floating in the Dam, as reported in our last issue. It appeared that the deceased was a fustian cutter, and formerly lived in Manchester. On Thurs- day evening, the 7th inst., deceased was met in Lymm by Mr. Thomas Holt, who took him to the house where he said he lodged, and left him on the 'door step. On Thursday morning deceased got lodgings with Mrs. Leigh, who, how- ever, lid not see him again although she heard someone knocking at the door late in the evening. About 7 o'clock" the following morning,llA body of the deceased w3s found in the Dam. A verdict of "-Found drowned " was returned , A I.YMM BUTCHER REMOVING CATTLE WITHOUT A LICENSE.—JaMPS FairChilZh, butcher, Lymm, and Edward Heasom, a boy in his employ, were summoned at the,Sale Sessions, on Monday, the former for causing to begemoved from an infected district (Lancashire) into Cheshire, cattle without a license; and Heasom for removing the animals. —Captain Little said the proceedings were taken under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act of 1878. He found Heasom driving three beasts through Altrincham on the sth July. Asked him for the license, and he produced one from the Manchester market authorit'es, but he had none for the county of Chester. He said the animals belonged to Mr. Fairclough. Foot-and-mouth disease had twice appeared at Lymm. and only on Saturday last were the premises declared free. In almost all cases of the kind the disease was trace- able to the removal of cattle.—Defendant said it was en- tirely against his wish to break the law ; he get the neces- ary licence at Manchester, and told the boy to get it en- dorsed at Sale. fie bad been in the habit of sending cattle by train.-4 tine of 108., including costs, was imposed in each case.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIAN.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday; present the Rev. J. W. N: Tanner; Messrs. John Ashton (in the chair), Lowe, Rigby, Nield, Acton, Jas. Darbyshire, Wright, Nornian, Handley, H. Linaker (clerk), awl W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.)

div.head: STATE OF THE HOUSE.
div.p: STATE OF THE HOUSE.

The MASTER'S report showed number of inmates in the house last week, 161, compared with 157 in oorresponding week last year; 596 posons had been relieved at a cost £6O, corresponding week last year, 655 persods at a cost of £63 10s. 9d. There were 29 boys and 28 girls in the Work- house school ; receiving industrial training 12 boys; 23 girls; total, 35.

M.R. LOWE AND THE ASYLUM. In the absence of Mr. Mclntyre, the CHAIRMAN proposed that a committee be appointed to visit the inmates of the County Asylum chargeable to the Union, to consist of the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Norman, Ch-alloner, Handley, and Linaker (clerk.)—Mr. LOWE thought the inmates might be left for another twelve months, without the chairman took some of the members who had not been there. Let them go in turns.—The CHAIRMAN: I merely propose this for Mr. Mclntyre—Mr. LOWE said it was •not required that they should go every year.—Mr. RIGBY concurred with Mr. Lowe.—Mr. LOWE inquired what the visit cost last year.—The CLERIC thought about 30s.— Mr. LOWE: I think it money sent away entirely.—Mr. RIGBY : Are these gentlemen in the habit of going every year?—The CHAIRMAN: I don't know . .

i'hat- they.' ire. They will be -guile" willing for some one else to take their places. Mr. LOWE : I don't want to go. I think it useless expendi- ture.—Mr. HANDLEY had no desire to go. The great bulk of the lunatics were from Runcorn, and when the visit was paid to see if any were fit to be removed, it was essential some one who knew them personally should be present.— Mr. LOWE said they were well looked after, a,pd the annual visit was not necissary.—Mr. HANDLEY remarked that Dr. Davidson had said that the Runcorn Guardians were the only union who appeared to care for their lunatics, and the visit had a beneficial effect upon the lunatics. Through the eft rts of the committee several persons had been removed from the asylum as sane, and It d continued so.—Mr. JAMES DARBYSHIRE thought it desirable the committee should pay the visit, and he did not like to hear hard expressions need against the lunatics.—The CHAIRMAN said being members of the union, the lunatics were treated the same as friends, and it was right that the Guardians should attend once a year to see how they were going on.— The CLERK said during the 18 years he had been clerk be bad been three times' and they were the most painful three days he ever had. (Hear, hear.—Mr. NORMAN remarked that he had been once.—Mr. LOWE : I have been a member longer than you and I have not been at all.—Mr. NORMAN had always thought two ought to be sent from Runcorn, one from Budworth, and one from Frodsham, as there were more lunatics from there than any other part.—Mr. LOWE: Most affecting !-The motion was darried, only Messrs. Lowe and Wright voting against it.

div.head: BOWLING COMPETITION AT HINTON.
div.p: BOWLING COMPETITION AT HINTON.
SIR A. B. WALKER'S CHALLENGE CUP.

The challenge cut presented to the Huvton Cricket and Bowling Club by Sir A. B. Walker, of Gateacre Grange, near Liverpool, was competed for for the seventh time by the members on Saturday last. The cup, which was manufac- tured by Elkington, Liverpool, and is worth about £3O, was given to thelub in 1875, and was won in that year by Mr. George Cunningham, in 1876 by Me.,C. Aldrich, in 1877 by Mr. G. Byrd, in 1878 by Mr. F. T. Turton' in 1879 by Mr. G. J. Paris, in 1880 by Mr. T. Graham, and this year by Mr. Ellison. The names of the respective winners are engraved on the outside of the cup, which is the third presented to the club by Sir Andrew, who is one of its Coldest,friends. The weather on Saturday was anything but favourable, rain descendiro, nearly the whole of the time the game was pro- ceeding. descending soaked condition of the ground naturally in- terfered with the bowling, and was exceedingly unpleasant to the players; but the inevitable was taken in good part, and on the whole everything passed off satisfactorily to all parties concerned. The attendance of spectators' especially b of tke fairer sex, was not so large as usual, but this was no doubt owing to the inclement state of the weather. Play commenced at four o'clock, but owing to the rain, which several times compelled the competitoYs to beat a hasty retreat to the welcome shelter of the pavilion, the game was not concluded until about eight o'clock, about an hour beyond the usual time. Of the previous winners of the cup, three competed, Messrs. Aldrich, Tortes, and Graham; of the other three, MeArs. Cunningham and Byrd are dead, and Mr. Paris is away owing to a serious illness in his family. In the first round Mr. Aldrich was defeated by Vr. Leyland, and in the third round Mr. Turton was beaten by Mr. Ellison, and Mr. Graham, one of the best bowlers in the club, in the same round, succumbed to the efforts of Mr. Wainwright. The latter bowled extremely well, and, at first, it was thought he would win the cup, but Mr. Ellison was in good form and played 80 accurately that the, former was defeated by six points. The following are the scores:—

At the cone] usion of the game a goodly eompany assembled at the rear of the tent to witness the presentation of the cup to the successful competitor. Mr. C. Aldrich said that, in the absence of the president and vice.president,he had great pleasure in handing over the cup to the winner, Mr. Ellison, the secietary of the bowling club, and he was quite certain there was no gentleman in that company who woul be more cordially recognised as the winner on that occasion than Mr. Ellison. That gentleman had undoubtedly dis- played, he might say, the greatest amount of ability as a ; bowler of any one in the club during the present season, but he had not, he believed, on any previous occasion, won a prize cup. Mr. EutsoN: Mr. Steel's, the vice-president's. I beg pardon, it was the president's. Mr. ALDRICH, continuing, said that was the second time Mr. Ellison had won .a prize cup. That cup had been won six times, and the names of the winners were engraved upon it, and Mr. Ellison's would be - the seventh name. If that gentleman should be so fortunate as to win it on the next occasion, he was sure they would all feel proud of his feat. He did not know whether Sir A. E. Walker had been made aware of a comne- tttion for his cup that, afternoon, but he believed he had. However, he was not present. Mr. Aldrich then handed the cup to the winner, remarking that he presented it to him to hold for one year, and hoped they would have as good a contest for it on many future occasions as they had had that day. (Applause.) Mr. EulsoN was very much obliged for their congratu- lations. His only regret was that he would have to bring it back again, and perhaps hand 41 °vr to somebody else. He wrote to Sir A. B. Walker informing him tbis prize cup would be played for that day, and Sir Andrew wrote back expressing his sorrow at not being able to attend, and stating that it would have afforded him much pleasure to have been at the competition, but, unfortunately' he had been for some time engaged to go with the Dock Board on their annual excursion, which took place on the same day. The proceedings then terminated.

At Gornal, on Monday, a number of operatives decided to resume work at an advance of 10 per cent., which resulted in their opponents seizing their tools and nails, and preyenting them from working. A disturbance of a serious character followed, and the police had to be called in to quell the riots.
Mr. Asher, Liberal, was on Wednesday, without opposi- tion, elected member for the Elgin Burghs, in roam of Mr. Grant Duff.

The wife of the vicar of Ansley, Nuneaton, has been savagely attacked by a dog. The lady was stooping down to feed a pet collie, which was tied to a kennel, when the animal suddenly seized her nose between its teeth, biting it in a most savage manner before it could be beaten off. The savage brute hid also bitten the lady's wrist and torn her clothing. The injuries inflicted are of a somewhat serious nature. It is assumed that the dog was mad at the time. IRON AND COAL TRADES.

Baunow-IN-Fnmeess, MONDAY. There is a steadier tone in the hematite pig iron trade, and the demand shows an improvement both on home and general foreign account, while prices also show an upward tendency. To-daYs busi- ness' was quiet, but large orders have been booked during the week, and the inquiry is very well maintained all round. No. 1 Bessemer• has improved to 595., and No. 3 to 57e.; this quotation eleo applies to No. 3 forge iron, which is selling well. There is a heavy outeut of metal, and although de- liveries have lately been comparatively large, stocka re- main very extensive all round. Indeed, makers have booked several new orders, and their mills both in the Bessemer rail and general merchant departments are busily employed. Iron ore is firmer in tone, and sales have lately been heavier. LANCASHIRE, WEDNESDAT.—But little material change can,be reported in the condition of the coal trade of this district. The market has all through continued extremely dull during the week, and very few of the Lancashire col- lieries are being kept going more than about half time The better qualities of round coal for house-fire purposes are still only in very limited demand, and with the exception of gas- making coals other descriptions of round coal continue generally a drug in the market, the requirements for the common sorts for steam and iron-making purposes being still , very much below the supplies offering by colliery proprietors. Stocks of round coal continue to accumulate heavily, and prices are so much 6overneO by the necessities of sellers who have to force these upon the market that actually fixed quo- tations are scarcely possible. The average prices at present being obtained for best coal at the pit month may be taken at about Se. to Ss. 6d., for seconds, 6s. to 6s. 9d., and for common classes of round coal, 48..9d. to ss. 31. per ton. Engine classes of fuel move off moderately well, but with the exception of the better qualities of slack the supplies in the market are generally much mere plentiful than had been anticipated, and prices are not more than maintained at late rates, burgy averaging about 4s. 3d. to 4s. Oct., and good slack 3s. 9d. to 4s. 3d. per ton at the pit mouth. In the shipping trade there is still an absence of activity, and common steam coal delivered at Liverpool or Gersten can be bought at prices ranging from 6s. 6d. to 7s. per ton. For coke there is a moderate demand, and some of the local makers are adopting improvements in their ovens with the I view of raising the quality of Lancashire coke for iron- , making purposes, and thus enabling it to compete with the Durham and other north-country makes. To some extent this is being accomplished, and local cokes of the better quali'y for iron-making purposes are now in some Cases fetching 15s. to 16s, per ton at the ovens, with inferior sorts averaging about 10s. to 12s. per ton. In the iron trade there has been somewhat of a lull during the last few days, due partly to the quarterly meetings taking place this week, but also in great measure to the fact that buyers have now mostly covered any immediate requirements, and are again apparently content to wait. A firm tone, however, is main- tained by sellers. and Lancashire makers of pig iron, who during the last few weeks have secured sufficient orders to carry them over the next three months, are not offering further in the market, pending the result of the quarterly meetings. The price of local pig iron can consequently only be given nominally at about 445. to 455. per ton, less 2i. per cent delivered equal to Manchester. Business in outside brands is still confined chiefly to Lincolnshire irons, and in these a few sales have been made at about the same figures as those quoted for local brands. A fairly improved busi- ness is still reported to be doing in the finished iron trade, Bars, hoops, and sheets are meeting with a tolerably good demand, chiefly for shipment; but with the exception of ham, for which in some cases an advanqe of 2s. 64. per ton has been asked during the week, no materially better prices are being obtained. For bars delivered into the Manchester district the average price is now abont £5 178.6 d., with some makers asking L 6 per ton. A better feeling is also noticeable amongst engineers and machinists; inquiries are made with more confidence, and lead more promptly to business than has been the case of late, but low prices are still being taken to secure new work.

ACCIDENT AT OVER.—The members of the Foresters' Club had their annual walk on Saturday last, preceded by the Over brass band. The didner was provided at the Blue Bell Inn, near St. Chars Church. During the proceedings a man named Joseph Bebbington by some means fell through the window in which he was seated, and in. his fall pullei another man, William Cheshire, with him. Bebbington was 'Much hurt, but it is feared Cheshire's injuries are more serious. He was taken to his home, where Dr. Okell is attending him. . . . .

ST. CHAD'S. OVER.—The choir of this church had their annual trip last Saturday, and chose ithyl as their destina- tion, where they enjoyed themselves much in the pretty scenery and on the splendid sands of that town.'

• VIE SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT WARRINGTON. , "DEALING WITH DANGEROUS STUFF." On Tuesday an ixquest was held in the Parade-room at the Police Station, before Mr. C. E.Driffield, coroner, on the body of a child named George Addison, who died shortly after one o'clock on Saturday morning last, as briefly Stated in last week's Examiner. Elizabeth Addison, a fustian cutter, living in Platt-street, said deceased was her child, and was four months old on the 3rd inst. He ate heartily enough on Friday last. Witness went to bed at hnlf-past ten o'clock at night, and her hus; band followed shortly afterwards. At half-past one o'clock she was giving the deceased something to drink, when she noticed that his hands were clenched, and that he stared at her. Her husband at once went for a doctor, and also celled in a neighbour, Mrs. Hayes, who took the child frem her. Witness had six children now living, and deceased wae the fifth 'child she had lost. Deceased was a small child, lent had not been under the care of a doctor. He had only had one fit. She was sure he had not met with any accident or been suffocated. Sarah Jane Hayes, of 12, Platt-street, said the child was dead when she saw it on Saturday morning. She undressed it, but there was nothing particularly noticeable about the colour of the flesh. There had been no nglect on the part of the parents. The mother and other neighbours used "infants' preservative." - Margaret Booth, wife of John Booth, joiner, Tilley-street, said she was maker of an infants' preservative, which she sold Wale neighbours at the rate of a half-pent* per bottle. Some days since one of Addison's children came to her fot a bottle of the preservative. She used a. pennyworth of lau- danum to a quart of water. The Coroner: You are deaiing• with danzerous stuff ;only I am glad to find that it is used at a safe strength. Witness: I have sold it for many years, and notomplaint . . has been Made yet. The Coroner: You most have the bottles labelled, and state the quantity of stuff to be taken. Witness: Very well, sir. It is very much in request. Children are often sent for it. The Coroner: The witness is responsible to whom she sells it. Witness: It cannot tlo harm. It would not hurt a child if it drank the contents of a full bottle. It would only send it to deep, as drink does a Loan who has had too much of it:

The Coroner : You must either give up selling the mix- ture, or you 'oust label the bottles: Let Inspector Proffitt see that the bottles are properly labelled. Witness: I will do so, but it will give me more trouble. The Coroner: Business is money, you know. A Juryman thought the mixture should be analysed by a doctor. ...The Coroner: Ifyou have any doubt about what the last witness has said, let the enquiry be adjourned; but if you take her statement on oath to be true, as I do, the child has not come to its death through taking her stuff. It was only a pennyworth of laudanum in a whole quart of water. The other drugs that are put in would have no effect at all. It would be absurd to think 'pat ,a pennyworth of laudanum put in a quart of water w6uld have any effect at all. But I understand from the Chief Constable that Mrs. Addison's house was in a dirty and,disgrEteeful condition.. . Inspector Proffitt: It was upstairs. . The Coroner: I think the jury may content themselves that the use of the stuff has had nothing whatever to do , with the child's death. I don't know when the last dose was given, but the mixture is so weak that it could not pos- sibly do harm. The jury then returned a verdict of "Found dead in bed from natural causes, probably from a convulsive fit."

THE EXHUMATION OF A BODY AT WTBUNBUICY, CHESHIRE.--TAL NantiViCh Petty Sessions, on Monday, Geo. Hayes, sexton ef the parish church of Wybunhury, was charged with the illegal burial of the child of Thomas Moulton, farmer, of the same parish. It may be remembered that an inquest was held on the body, which was exhumed, and the coroner made some strong remarks both as to the conduct of the sexton and of the father. The defendant now admitted that he buried the child without a certificate from a medical man, Moulton stating that it was stillborn, and that he would afterwards forward the certificate. Moulton said the child only lived twenty-four hours, and he told the sexton it was stillborn, and said he would send the certificate. Defendant said he had been sexton for thirty years, and acted through ignorance. The bench took th•ts view 0 f the case, and bound defendant to come up 00 his own recognisances when tvilled on, be paying all expenses.
