div.head: MASTER'S REPORT.
div.p: MASTER'S REPORT.

The MASTER reported the number of inmates at the end of last week to be 494, previous week 500, corresponding week last year 518. There were 145 children at Kirkdale Schools. —The Rev. Father Kiernanof Rain kill, had sent a large parcel of illustrated papersokc., for the inmates —lt was .1 resolved that a vote of thanks be give to Father Kiernan.

div.head: LETTER FROM THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.
div.p: LETTER FROM THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.

The CLERK stated that be had received a letter from the Local Government lirard relative to the vaccination con- tracts for the Hale and Wootton districts, and asking that particulars of the arrangements the Guardians proposed to snake for vaccination in the Huyton district, might he for- warded for approval. The letter was ordered to stand over till a definite arrangement had been arrived at.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF THE PORTER. AND FORTRESS.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF THE PORTER. AND FORTRESS.

! The following letter was read from the porter and j portress :—" Gentlemen,—We beg most respectfully to !tender our resignation of the offices of porter and portress of your Union Workhouse. We have received the appoint- ment of master and matron of Tewkesbury Workhouse, and ' have been requested to otter upon the duties on Monday, the.lBth instant. We should feel obliged if you would re- lieve us from oar duties from that date. Thanking you sin- cerely for the courtesy and kindness we have received at Your hands, we beg to remain, gentlemen, your obedient ser- vants, T. B. and E. SELLIVAN."—The CLERK stated that the Guardians of Tewkesbury Workhouse required an ex- pression of opinion of the Guardians of the Presc,t Union as to Mr. Sullivan's capabilities as a workhouse master.—lt Ivas resolved that a testimonial be given to Mr. Sullivan. ALLEGED GROSS IMPOSITION AT ST. HELENS.

The CLERK read the following communication from Mr. Stuart. relieving officer of the St. Helens No. 1 district:— "I wish to report to you the following case of gross im- position, and to ask if you do not think it a case in which a prosecution should follow. On the sth July, James Taylor, 136, Park-road, Parr, applied to 'me for relief, owing to having broken his arm. representing that he had a wife and six children, one of whom Was earning about 3s. 6d. per week on the pit brow. He had only been working a few days at the pit himself when he met with the accident which broke his arm, consequently he was not en- titled to any relief from the pit club. Owing to his repre- sentations I gave him a ticket for food to the value of ss. This day (July 9th) he came to my house during the dinner hour bearing the enclosed letter from Mr. Buckley. lat first refused to give any further relief until* I had visited the house, but upon his representing that his wife had been confined this morning, was very bad, and that there was nothing to eat in the house for her and the children, I returned with him to the office and gave him a . .

ticket, value Os., and determined to visit the case at once. I did so, reaching the house in about half an hour from the time the man was at my house. I there found the min's wife in good health, not having been confined (nor likely to be so far as my observations went), annome eggs and bacon in process of cooking. I had much trouble in eliciting re- plies to any of my questions to the wife. The daughter, aged 14, acknowledged to earning is. 3d. per day at Groves s colliery, and although the man had stated he had six children, I only saw four. The mother gave me the names of six, stating that the other two were out somewhere. Shortly after leaving the house I met Mr. Buckley, who also had been making inquiries, and from what he had learnt was endeavouring to find out where the man was likely to obtain his goods from, so that lie (Mr. Buckley) might order the tradesmen not to supply the goods, feeling cinvincect that the man had imposed upon him. I afterwards called at Mrs. Middlehursts' to inquire if Taylor had vet been for his goads. I was told "Yes, but he has not taken them all ; only 35. 3d. worth of flour and is going to send for the remainder." I forthwith altered the ticket t 035. 3d. so that Taylor should not obtain any more goods upon it. Mrs. Middiehurst shortly afterwards followed me to the office to inform me that Taylor had not received 3s. 3d. worth of flour, but by the same statements as he had previously made to me had induced Mrs. Middlehurst to give him 3s. 34. in money, stating that the midwife was in his house and that the money was required for her. Such is the case I have to report. Do you think that the man should be proceeded against for 'obtaining relief under false pretences ?"—On the motion of Mr. PARIS, seconded by Mr. TYREE, it was resolved that Taylor be ploBecute4.—Mr. MEADOWS hoped Mr. Stuart would be able to prove his case this time.—Mr. PIDIIER said it should be distinctly understood by the Board that Mr. Stuart or any other relieving officer of the Union who took a case before the magistrates, should have the assistance of Mr. Hartley, the clerk, and else legal assistance if necessary.—Mr. Tyrer proposed that the relieving officers be instructed never, in future, to Ante a ticket to any pro- vision dealer who had given money to a pauper in lieu of provisions in exchange for the ticket.—The proposition was agreed to, on the understanding that it would not amply to this particular case.

THE COST OF OUT-DOOR RELIEF IN THE UNION. The CLERK referred to statistics of pauperism ot various unions supplied to him by Mr. Basil Cane Government In- spector, and he was sorry to say that the Preseot Union almost stood first in the expenditure for out-door relief. For the twelve months ended Lady Day last the cost of out- door relief in the Preseot Union amounted to £11,795.

div.head: BUILDING COMMITTEE.
div.p: BUILDING COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the Building Committee, held on July 13th, a letter from Messrs. Weeks and Hughes, respecting the offer to them of 150 guineas as compensation for their services in connection with schools, was read, and it was resolved that no further offer be made to them.—The com- mittee recommended the adoption of Benham's scheme for new bakehouse at an estimated cost of £276 15e,, and the clerk was authorised to take the required steps for obtaining the sanction of the Local Government Board, and if neces- sary fi.r borrowing the money.—lt was moved and seconded that the minutes be passed.—Mr. MEADOWS movad, and Mr. PARIS seconded, that the minutes be passed excepting that part referring to the new bakehouse.—On being put to the meeting, the original motion was carried by 13 to 5.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

_ At a meeting of this committee on the 13th inst. the clerk produced a return showing the relieving officers' districts land salaries in 33 other unions and parishes, and it was re- solved that the salaries of Messrs. Goff and Parkinson be in- creased by £2o.—Letters from Dr. McNicoll, medical officer, St. Helens, respecting the proposal to add £5 to his salary, land asking that the subject be reconsidered, were read. It was recommended that the salary be in future £9O per annum. A letter was read from Mr. Sherratt, shoemaker at the Workhouse, asking for an increase of wages, but the con- sideration of the same was deferred.—The question of the borrowing of £1,600 for erection of chapel and alteration of schools was postponed.—Mr. HALL moved, and Mr. FIDLER seconded the confirmation of the minutes, and Mr. Hall gave notice of motion that at the next meeting he would move that the sajaries of Messrs. Goff and Parkinson, relieving officers, should be increased £2O each, making £l2O per annnm ; that Dr. McNicoll, medical officer, St. Helens, be granted an increase of .415, making the salary £9O per annum; and that the resolution respecting guarantee societies be rescinded.
APPOINTMENT OF POOR-RATE COLLEtTORS FOR BOLD AND
WIIISTON.

At a special meeting of the Guardians held on the 13th inst., to consider the applications for collector of poor-rates for the Bold and Whistou districts, several candidates were selected to appear before the Board at their nest meetißg : James Houghton was appointed collector for Bold district at a salary of £43 per annum. and Edmund Range, Prescot, was appointed collector for Whiston district at a salary of Z3O per annum.

t 5 driverj s t nh go rwabent 'TRAVELS IN TIIE EAST. tah:a In: dt 1: se taCrld , sprang forward and kept her on the saddle. Two or three of riboeirvuoseeaset,otatshsohAe bulita‘foerl-ct)hste the gentlemen who were not accustomed to donkey-back or loose saddles, found themselves under the donkeys bellies, , and even the stoutest of our little party caught his foot in dismounting and went rolling in the "barbaric mad." We had quite a catalogue of disasters to enliven the dinner table,, and give zest to our appetites. The donkey boys in Cairo ng are a curious sharp witted race. They will follow the whole length of a street pressi their donkeys upon you. "This They s distinguish eem to from an American or Frenchman. "This isnot you at once is vair good donkey, mistare!" " Yankee Doodle, mistare—this .is Johnny ; or " this is Ginger Bob'—vair good donkey ass, naistare!" To show bow they catch hold of even our slang expressions, one , of them in Alexandria offered to take me .to Pompey's I pillar for a "bob." 1 saw a terrible fight between two Arab boys in the open street. The fiendish character.of the encounter still makes me shudder when I think of it. When I first saw them the bigger of the lads whose own throat was bleeding, had his fingers clutching the throat of the other, as belay on his back. After a desperate wriggle the under one got free, and continued to struggle with his adversary at arm's length, waiting for his advantage. Just then a tall Arab came up and interfered; when the smaller boy finding the other off his guard, sprang with his hard head right at his month, stunning him for a moment while the blood spirted from his lips. The fixed eye, the pallid look of deadly hate with which they regarded each other, as they walked side by side, ready for another spring, was a picture of Oriental savagery I shall never forget. On Sunday morn- ing, February 27th, we visited the Coptic quarter, and ex- pected to witness the worship in one of the Coptic churches; but we were too late the people were coining out soon after ten o'clock. We walked into the place, and were each pre- sented with one of the small loaves given away by the Patriarch, to those who do not commune,—l suppose as a token of good-will to Christian and Barbarian alike. The bread has symbolic figures impressed upon it. In the centre Christ is repre3ented, and tround Him the twelve apostles. Around the border are letters in the Coptic language render- ing praise to Christ. One of the deacons entered into a bale. explanation of his church's creed. We gathered that the system was one of Monotheism, in which Christ was the supreme and only God; that they believed in His divine, hut not in His human nature; that they immersed both infants and adults on receiving them into the church; that penances abounded; and that in nearly all respects, aside from their adoration of Christ as the only God, they are an Egyptian Greek church, or perhaps taking into account the chanting and horning of incense, ringing of bells, etc., the system May be regarded as a mixture of Greek and Roman Chris- tianity. The Coptic ladies dress in the same style as the Mahommedan—veiled and enveloped in the large sheet ; but the gown below which they take care to exhibit, is usually of a gaudy coloured silk, such as crimson or ovant!e, puce, or green of the brightest tints. Unlike the Mabommedan ladies, they move quite freely about the streets, waddling, for the most part, under a weight of corporeal obesity, which, though esteemed their highest beauty, must be sufficiently distressing in so hot a climate as Egypt. Thanking ttie deacon, who almost implored us to come again, for his courtesy, we hastened to the English Episcopal Church, where we found a neat new edifice, capable of bolding about 150 people, nicely filled. The sermon was short, pithy, and practical ; and the singing very simple and sweet. (To be continued next week.)

BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [Spactet.] No. VII. CAIRO AND THE PYRAMIDS. The morgue of Mehemet All, which stands within the walls of the citadel, is another of those huge hecatombs in the building and decorating of which the life-blood of the peop:e has been so lavishly expende3 ; yet its erec- tion is regarded as the crowning glory of IVlehemet Al's reign. Doubtless, the end of his ambition'—to lie the moA -.th its splendid dome—has been

honoured of all, beneaa.. sph. realised. The grand temple built.of Oriental alabastex, and adorned with the most costly magnificence, covers his re- in tins, and is called by his name. But what then? Shall this one memorial cover as with a mantle, the remembrance of all his crimes? Nay, is this one memorial not in itself a crime? May not the grinding oppression, the prolonged injustice that drained the price of it out of an already peeled and down-trodden people, for over stand before high heaven as the darkest blot on Mehemet Ali' blood-stained escut- cheon! On the battlements of the citadel is shown the place from which the Mameluke officer leapt with is hors., a height of 85 feet, when Mehemet All, having in- , vited 500 Matnelukes to a bancoet, surrounded them by his soldiers in this broad area, and butchered them in cold blood, following up the inhuman slaughter by the extermi- nation or banishment of all the Mamelukes in Cairo. This vigorously ani successfully performedr, proved deed has s metimes been applauded as a great act of politi- cal amputation, Mehemet All commended as having by such means p himself a wise sovereign—the saviour and regenerator of Egypt. Poor Egypt, with such men as ber'saviours and regenerators! Does it not come to this: that when blee,l- - purging, and blistering fails to make a nation quiescent under misrule and oppression, some imperial sangrado— more bold than the rest—may come forward and remove the only limb that shows any sign of life for fear of the patient getting restive, and giving him increased trouble? Through the same years that Mehemet All was wading through seas of blood to accomplish his reforms, our own country was in the•throes of political anarchy, perhaps as keen as theirs. But bow aifferent the m ,thods our reformers pursued, and how different have been the results! By removing disabili- ties, equalising our country's laws, and improving her insti- tutions, hostile factions were disarmed one after another, until now, strength, stability, and increasing vitality reign through the Constitution; while poor Egypt, bleeding and tortured, can scarcely lift her languid eye to look upon the great alabaster mausoleum which was drained out of her heart's blood, and contains the ashes of her self .glorified oppressor. Joseph's well is also within the walls of the ' and from it the citadel is supplied with water. listir

their worships as to whether it was necessary for him to prove anything further than the award of the arbitrator, who had considered the apportionment against defendant. The proper notices had been given to defendant, the work had been done, and the expenses awarded. Seddon 69 of the Act of Parliament, dealing with the question provided for the recovery of the expenses, and in oase of dispute the matter was to be referred to arbitration. In this case there had been such a dispute, and it had been referred to arbitration. The proceedings in the present instance were brought under the 123 section of the Act of 1848.—Me Charles Allcard produced the copy of a notice, dated the 27th June, 1873, which had been served on the defendant. The plans of the sewerage were made and deposited in accordance with the Act of Parliament.—Mr. Higginson, surveyor to the Board, produced the plan for sewering the defendant's property in Oakland-street, and said it was approved by the Local Government Board at the time. Before such approval it was open for the in- spection of any person interested, as provided by the Act.— Mr. Allcard was again placed in the box, and said he was surveyor to the Board in July, 1874, and the work to which the apportionment related Was done by the Board, the property being of a private character.—Mr. Higeinson said he was appointed surveyor to the Board in May, 1875, and he apportioned the expenses as to the Oakland-street property. The total amount of the apportionment was £579 Os. 4d., and the defendant's share of this was £46 Ils. 9d.—Mr. Thomas Hughes proved serving the necessary notices on the defendant; and Mr. Robert W. H. Thomas, solicitor, St. Helens, said the signature produced wee the one he made as attesting witness of the award by Mr. Wilson.—Mr. John Knowles said he served the demand upon the defend- ant on the 7th May last. —Mr. Prest then asked that an order might he made upon the defendant for payment of the sum claimed and costs.—The Chairman said he thought the magietratrs could not make any order as to costs. The Local Board had their own clerks and establishment, and their powers were certainly somewhat arbitrary.—Mr. Prest replied that in such cases it was usual to grant costs. The expenses with which defendant was charged had been owing a long time, and the Local Boards were as much entitled to their costs as anybody else. The Board were representing the interests of the ratepayers in this matter, and if people like the defendant would not pay what they were clearly bound to do, there was no reason in the world why the ex- pensee of taking proceedings against them should come out of the pockets of the taxpayers.— The Chairman: He should have paid this long ago, and then the costs would hot have been so heavy, perhaps.—Mr.Preat said that the case had only been settled agreeably on defendant consenting to pay the costs. which had been reduced to 42a.—The Chairman said that under those circumstances he thought they might make the order for costs.—The next case taken was one against Mr. J. Hedlev, for £6los. 2d., sewerage expenses.—Mr. Prest repre- sented the Local Board in this and the following cases, and Mr. Slater (Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., Warrington), appeared for the defendants.—Mr. Allcard was called, and said the defendant's apportionment also related to Oakland- street. Tfte work had been done by the Board.—Mr. Slater, for the defence, said that in this action there had been no dispute as to the apportionment, which had never been questioned, but the whole liability of the defendant to pay the amount had been denied. Theee was no authority in the Act of 1875, or of any other Act, to empower the Board to proceed to arbitration when the total liability was disputed, and not merely the apportionment. —Mr. Prest, on the contrary, submitted that the only power which the Local Board had under the Act was to deal with the apportionment and then proceed under the 25th section to recover the amount.—The Magistrates' Clerk: You see, Mr. Slater, that there is merely a dispute as to whether the work ;las been done, and not as to the ap- portionment —Mr. Prest: It has been admitted that this award has been inade.—Mr. Slater: But naturally if my ob- jection holds good, the award is bad.— Mr. Prest: I hold that the award of the arbitrator is conclusive.—The Magis- trates' Clerk : The justices could not possibly go into the question of whether the work was done or not, or as to the charge being a fair or an unfair one. Such matters would have to go before the Local Board.—The Bench made an order for the payment of the sum claimed and the costs of the barrieter.—The next case called was one of a similar summons against Mr. Wedgewood Thomas, the original claim being £BO, and this had been increased to £ll5. Mr. Slater again disputed the entire liability of his client. The magistrates' clerk remarked that if defendant had disputed something shove that referred to in the notice sent to film by the Board, he ought to have specified what it was.—Mr. Sister: The great idea of the Act is -- .—The Magistrate? Clerk : The "Great idea of the Act" will not come in hero! The Act says that un- less the defendant gives notice that he disputes the appor- tionment, it will be binding; and if he want2cl to say that be did not diepute the apportionment, but the whole thing upon which it was founded, then he should- have gone on to say so.—Mr. Prest wished the Beach to know that the Local Board had not acted in en overbearing manner in any of these matters, and he gave instances with the object of proving this statement. —ln reply to the Magistrates' Clerk, Mr. Slater admitted that the only 'defence he had to offer was that he had already laid befqie the magistrates.—The Bench then made an order for payment of the full aenount claimed and the barrister's costs.—Mr. Midwood, of Davies-street was summoned for non-payment of £ll 17s. 3d. under similar circumstances, and the Bench also made an order for ayment in this else, and the costs of Mr. Prest.

div.head: – 17,IC.:LAINE11, SATURDAY, JULY 16 1881. RUNCORN BOARD OF COM MISSIQN ERS.
div.p: - 17,IC.:LAINE11, SATURDAY, JULY 16 1881. RUNCORN BOARD OF COM MISSIQN ERS.

The adjourned meeting of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners was held on Monday, for the purpose of con- sidering the position of the Board as to Waterloo House. Dr. Steele presided, and there were also present Messrs. Lyon, Norman, McDougall, Philip Speakman, Handley, Taylor, Briscoe, Marshall, Hazlehurst, Mearlowcroft, Williams, Brookes (secretary), Linaker (law-clerk), and Barker (surveyor). TIIE BOARD AND WATiRLOO ROUSE. Mr. P. SPRABBAN proposed that the Commissioners should refer the question of deciding what should be done with the house to the committee which had been appointed to lo after the properties of the Board.—Dr. Mellor:ram:L. thought they should advertise the building for letting or selling.— to do anything with

Mr, HANDLEY said they had no power __, ......jg w,,, the house other than use it for hospital purposes.—The CHAIRMAN thought they could get the consent of the Local Government Board to use the building as an hospital.—Dr. McDrinniatt. said it had been occupied by a private tenant for four years, and until now tNey bad not heard any objec- tion against the house being diverted from its proper pur- pose.—Mr. Nerman seconded the proposition. MR. MARSHALL MAKES THE MIRROR HONORABLE. At this "part of the proceedings. Mr. George Marshall entered the room, and the Cnettinats said that at their last meeting Mr. Marshall said he knew that he had insulted the chair, and he (Dr. Steele) now thceight that it was due he should apologise. It was also reported in the newspapers that Mr. Marshall used the rernark.—Mr. Miasmata.: I do not want to enter into a de- bate on this question except you withdraw your remarks, Mr. Chairman. If you will withdraw your observations then I will withdraw mine. It was not my desire to insult you or any other member of the Board, and I think L have always shown a wish in that direction. But when you come forward without giving me any notice of your intention to discuss the matter—excuse me explaining the circum- stances—instead of approaching Me in a gentlemanly manner, I think it is time to defend myself. That is all, sir; and if you will withdraw your remarks then I will do the sine—The Law CLERK: What remarks do you refer to, Mr. Marshall.—Mr. MARSHALL having explained the observations to which Le alluded, the CHAIRMAN addressing that gentleman, said: I made no remark about you, and I have nothing to withdraw. As the Chairman of this Board ,I shall not, while I sit here, hear anything more Mr. Marshall may have to say unless he complies with my request.—Mr. HAZLEHERST: lam glad this subject has been mentioned, because it gives those members who were not pre.ent an opportunity of remarking upon the proceed- ings. I think there is hardly anyone here who is not smarting under the lash of the report that appeared in the newspapers of last Monday's meeting. I think nothing so humiliating, so pitiable. so undignified, and so utterly dis- graceful has ever appeared in the reports connected with the town; and the question as to whether the Vyrnwy ticket belong esi to this man or that man is utterly insignificant in di ice that has been inflicted upon ..- .

HEALTII COMIITTEE.--LOW DEATII-RATE. The minutes of the Health Committee were approved on the proposition of Mr. CAREY. They showed that the births for the month had been 72, or 345 per thousand; and deaths 20, or 96 per thousand. Thu latter included four children under one year, and seven between one and five years. There had been three deaths from zbmotic diseases. There had been a further complaint as to "Mr. GloVer's works, and that gentleman stated that he had not dried any sulphate of lead since Whitsuntids.—The following are the vaccination re- turns for the year endik December 31st, 1880: Number of births registered 1,196, succesifully vaccinated, 881, dead unvaccinated 130, postponed by medical certificate 27, can- not be found 65, unsusceptible 0, defaulters 93.—The mar- ket receipts for June showed a decrease amounting to £5 17s 3cl as compared with June last year.—At &meeting on the sth inst., the Surveyor submitted a specifiCation and estimate for painting and lime-washing the market. The Committee, having inspected the hall, came to the conclusion that paint- ing was not at present absolutely requisite, and might be de- . . • • • be do-

. . feed, and that the requisite lime-washing might by the Board's workmen (Ca piece work, if found 'advan- tageous), and the Surveyor was instructed accordingly, and to have all necessary glazing in the roof done. FINANCE.-MR. BEASLEY'S ACCOCNT. At a meeting of the Finance Committee, on the 7th inst., the Law Clerk's bills for the past five years, as referred to the Clerk of the Peace, and which had been taxed and allowed at £1,789 14s. 7d., were produced. £742 15s. &L et this amount having been previously charged to the various accounts it was resolved that the balance of £1,046 19s. ld. he apportioned as follows - West bank promenade, £7 7s. 2d.; main sewerage scheme, £2 18s. 10d.; market capital account, £69 10s. 101; Birchfield-road. £5O 3s. 104.; Milton-road, £23 135.; Victoria-road, £64 3s. 24.; Albert. road, £4 19..; Appleton property, £l7 6s. 21.; Moorfield- lane, £9 104. 24.; Derby-road, £l2 18s.; Church-street (Pit-lane). £5 7s. Bd.; Warrington-road, £6 6s. Od.; survey account, £1 4s. 21.; water extension account, £9 45. 61.; gas capital, £2l 6s. 44.; water revenue account, £287 Os. 6c1.; health committee expenditure, £l3 6s. 24.; legal expenses account, £417 16s. id.; property improvement suspense ac- count, West-bank sewerage, £22 175.; total, £1,046 193 id. Against this sum there has been advanced £261 45., leaving the net amount due to him £785 15s. ld.-It was also re- solved that the following cheques (Mr. Beasley assenting) be drawn upon the Treasurer, and debited to Mr. Beasley:-- Parr's Banking Co., £2l 6s. 44.; Lewin and Gregory, £2lO Us 44.; Mr. Kennedy, £l2 65., Mr. Pickford, Mr. C. 11. Beloe, £lO 18s.; Parr's Banking Co., £5O lie.; on water eitlension account-Pares Banking Co., £9 48.6 d.; on treasurer's general account-Mr. Seger, £7O 18s. 64.; Parr's Banking Co., £349 3s. 11d.; J. W. Wareing and Co., £44 4s. 61; total, £785 15s. id. According to this state- ment the whole amount due to the Law Clerk will be swal- lowed up in the payments.-Instructions had been given for such steps to be taken as may be necessary to recover Mr. Carlile's account as to Market-street. The minutes were passed on the proposition of Mr HAYES, seconded by Mr. Gaskxx.L. MR ALLEN APPOINTED CLERK. This Company is formed for the purpase of erecting works, and carrying on the business of Salt and Chemical Manufac- turers, on a very.extensive scale, at afiddlewich, in the County of Chester. and generally for the purports specified in the Memorandum of Association. Greet Salt deposits exist at Middlewich and ether places in the County of Chester, and bri e is raised or pumped trom these deposits, and manufactuied by evaporation into salt for home and foreige crivisumption. In addition to over half a , million tons used at borne over one million tons were exported last year The Cheshire salt district yields by far the greatest postio.: of the supply; in fact, it has practically the monopoly of supplying the world with salt, furnishing, as it does, 1 000,000 tons per annum for expert 'from Liverpool, arid up- wards of 400,000 thus to the chemical works of Widnes and other towns. There can be no doubt that the salt trade is one of the mast Important mineral hidustina: 4s the kingdom. The trade is also a most profitable one. The manufacture of cherub. ,t which salt is most exten- sively used, is also a very profit:. - utininess.. For the -commencement of op.:. .• '.es an eligible site, con- ' taming aboutfive a half acres, ori ws, •Is valuable brine springs or runs exist, situate at Riudeiton, al ii rich. in the County of Chester, and adjacent both to canal aNd railway, has been I ' secured for the first works of the Company on advantageous I terms, the purchase money for which (R 20,04.0 will be Paid by the allcitment to the Vendors of 1,400 fully paid-up Ordinary , Shares, and the I alanoe (E 13,000 in cash. The estate Is freehold, and beneath the surface of the soil lea I very fine bed of clay, fr, m which all the bricks for the erection of the necessary works and buildings canbe made. This will save a considerable outlay in the cost of the works. On one portion of the estate there is a valuable bed of sand, which Can be used in the building of the proposed works of the Company. There is also a large mansion and outbuildings, suitable for the residence of a Manager and for the Company's offices on the I estate. The Company will be prepared to adopt the best machinery, methods, and pa...ents which may be invented from time to , time for the manufacture of both _aft and chemicals. This Company will raise the brine for salt snaking from its own land, and will thus save the royalty or rate of 61, per ton of salt ordinarily paid by sad makers in the district for brine. This alone will effect a great saving in the manufacture of salt of this Company; and. in addition to lids, the saving in the price of the cost and carriage of salt to be used in the manufac- ture of chemicals by this Company (salt having to be purchased by other chemical marufactures) will be Any great The Salt Works at both Northwich and Winsford are subject to occasional stoppages and to great damage and disablement, caused by subsidences of the la d. in consequence of the large , and cent-noel extraction of salt-rock and brine therefrom. The ,•Works of this Company will be erect ed upon solid virgin ground. some miles distant from these sinking places. The brine at Middlewich is also of a better class and of greater strength for salt mairleg purposes then that got either at Northwich or, Winsford, and • a new source of supply such as the one now proposed to .be worked will be of incalcu- lable value. The site ef the proposed Works, being in else proximity to to the Trent and Mersey Canal. and abutting or the London and IN 01111-WP.,"'" 'railway, this compasty can lead its MlMl- alto railway wagons at the Works, and will be able to save a considerable antount paid by 'other manufacturets at Middlewich for catnaps to the rail- way. The subsequent erection or purchase of other works at suit- able places in the district is also contemplated. Tire existing salt and chemical works in the Cheshire districts are ding prosperous and increasing trades, arid from the known remunerative character of both businesses the Directors are of opinion that the Share Capital of this Company will even in times of depression In trade earn a minimum profit of 15 per cent. per annum, and that these dividends in active seasons will be largely increased, and their are satisfied that the shares of this Company will be a sound and lucrative investment. It is estimated that the prssent issue of capital will be amply sufficient to enable the Directors to complete the pur- chase of the estate named, and to erect and finish works thereon to a large and paying extent, as well as provide a sufficient surplus with which to commence business. The vendors of the site and brine spriegs already selecled for the first works of the Company are so satisfie 1 with the pros- pects of the undertaking that they have agreed to deposit ordi- nary fully paid up shares rf the C onpany to the value of £7,000 with rho D rectors for two y••ars, as a security for tbe payment. of a dividend of 7# per cent, per annum on the pre- iereuce shares of the Company. Applb ation will be made irs due course to the Stock Ex- change for MI official quotation of the shares of the Company. The only agreements entered into are one for the purchase of the freehold site and brine springs at Xinderton.
